Quick Answer
Google Maps’ Ask Maps turns travel planning into a chat. It can build full itineraries, answer questions about places, suggest personalized nearby spots, plan surprise trips, and compare routes, travel times, costs, and transport options using Maps data.
Almost every app, website, or product has AI features now. While most AI implementations were forced, some of them are genuinely useful. I really loved the AI integration in Notion, where it simplified the hardest part of creating databases. Very recently, Hostinger’s implementation of the support agent is very useful for performing actions with just simple natural prompts. Finally, the Google Maps “Ask Maps” feature is what I really liked as the best AI implementation after those.
For those who are unaware, Google has rolled out the “Ask Maps” feature in Google Maps, which lets you chat with the application just like any LLM.
In simple words, you can chat with Google Maps for directions, information about places, calculate distances between places, basically everything you already do with Google Maps but in a more conversational format.
Table of Contents
5 Ways ‘Ask Maps’ Makes Google Maps Much More Useful
The best part of this implementation is that it works all the time and is very reliable. If you use Google Maps or even Apple Maps, I highly recommend trying this feature.
Since Google Maps is also available for iPhones, it is my default map app on the iPhone too. If you are using an older version, you can update Google Maps to the latest version by clicking on the links below.
Once you are done, here is everything you need to know about the Ask Maps feature, how to use it, and five unique ways to get the most out of it.
Plan Complete Trips With Accurate, Real-Time Information
There are plenty of AI trip planners out there that are very reliable, but Google Maps has a significant edge over them with its huge, real-time, and accurate amount of data.
I believe most of those applications also use Google Maps data for place suggestions, but you get everything for free with accurate details inside Google Maps.
And since this is an AI feature, just like any AI chat, you can have as many conversations as you want and personalize it the way you want.
You can ask everything about places, time, reviews, how much time it’s going to take, best alternatives, timings, and everything else while planning a trip.
For the best output, you can just copy and paste the prompt below with your details into Google Maps to get a detailed plan of whatever trip you are planning.
The best part is, Google also offers a preview of your destinations on the real map. You can see the list of all the places you are going to visit, the route you want to go through, and much more.
Since this can be a continuous conversation, you can follow up with new plans or any changes to your plans; it will automatically calculate and replan your entire journey based on the changes you want.
Prompt to Plan a Complete TripPlan a complete trip from [starting location] to [destination] for [number of days or dates].
My preferences:
- Budget: [budget]
- Traveling with: [solo/family/friends/couple]
- Interests: [nature, food, beaches, temples, shopping, nightlife, photography, etc.]
- Preferred transport: [car/public transport/walking/bike]
- Preferred pace: [relaxed/moderate/packed]
Create a day-by-day itinerary using places available on Google Maps.
For every place, include:
- Why it is worth visiting
- Best time to visit
- Opening hours
- Approximate time needed there
- Distance and travel time from the previous stop
- Best transport option
- Rating and important review highlights
- Estimated cost if available
- Nearby restaurants or food options
- Good alternatives if the place is closed or crowded
Arrange the places in the most practical order so I don’t waste time traveling back and forth.
At the end, show all the places on a route and give me a short summary of total travel time, approximate distance, and the most important things I should know before starting the trip.
Ask Anything About a Place Before You Visit
Another most useful feature for me in Google Maps is “Ask about a place.”
Previously, before Ask Maps, Google introduced “Ask about this place,” where you could just ask anything, and based on the reviews, it would answer your questions.
But ever since Ask Maps introduced it, you can just have conversations about any place, including learning about the place and what others think about it using real user reviews.
Not just that, you can also ask anything about multiple places, compare them, and much more.
For instance, you can ask how much time it would take to get to a certain point, what the timings, holidays, and do’s and don’ts are, what the negative reviews say, what recent incidents have happened around that place, the closest alternatives to that place, and everything else and much more.
The best part is it takes real data as input and answers your questions.
Prompt to Ask Everything About a PlaceTell me everything I should know before visiting [place name].
Use the latest information available in Google Maps and organize the answer clearly.
Include:
- What the place is known for
- Why people visit it
- Current opening and closing hours
- Best time of day to visit
- Best days to visit
- Entry fee or other costs if available
- How long people usually spend there
- Parking availability
- Public transport options
- Accessibility information
- Food and restaurants nearby
- Restrooms and other useful facilities
- Things I should carry
- Important rules, restrictions, or things visitors should avoid
- Common complaints from reviews
- Most positive things recent reviewers mention
- Whether it is suitable for families, kids, elderly people, couples, or solo visitors
- Safety or practical concerns
- Nearby places I can combine with this visit
Also suggest 3 good alternatives nearby and explain why I might choose each one instead.
Find Personalized Places Near You
Google Maps’ “Near me” feature is very helpful to quickly find places in your location, such as restaurants, living places, public transport, and much more. But this gets even better with personalized results using the “Ask Maps” feature.
Previously, the “Near Me” feature showed the exact same results for everyone, with no option to customize or personalize them. But with the “Ask Maps” feature, you can personalize locations and get dynamic results based on your needs.
For instance, if you only want a list of affordable hotels near you, you can simply ask Google Maps to show you just those. Plus, you can ask for locations that are currently open, locations that are a particular distance away from you, or even locations with specific needs. And again, the possibilities are endless. You can customize it the way you want.
Prompt to Find Personalized Places Near YouFind the best [restaurants/hotels/cafes/parks/attractions/etc.] near me based on these requirements:
- Maximum distance: [distance]
- Budget: [budget]
- Minimum rating: [rating]
- Must be open: [now/specific time]
- Preferred features: [parking, family-friendly, quiet, AC, outdoor seating, WiFi, etc.]
- Things I want to avoid: [crowded places, expensive places, poor parking, etc.]
Do not just give me the most popular places.
Compare the best options using Google Maps information and reviews.
Create a table with:
- Place name
- Distance from me
- Travel time
- Rating
- Price level
- Opening hours
- Why you recommend it
- Biggest positive mentioned in reviews
- Biggest complaint mentioned in reviews
- Who the place is best for
Then recommend the best overall option for my requirements and explain why.
Plan a Surprise Weekend Trip Based on Your Interests
Some say unplanned trips are the best, and it’s absolutely true in my case. If I plan everything, it doesn’t happen. My best trips are unplanned. Also, I really wish there was a button that I could randomly press on the weekend and visit the place it suggests.
With the Ask Maps feature, you can do exactly that. You can just open Ask Maps and plan a surprise trip this weekend, personalizing it with your own wishes, such as being close to nature, a beach vibe, mountains, hiking, a road trip, and much more.
Based on your location and the time you leave, Google Maps suggests an important place.
You can have continuous conversations about the place to plan the perfect trip. However, if you want to just visit a random location without asking questions, you can do that too.
To do that, open Google Maps, tap on the Ask Maps feature, and enter this prompt. And that’s it.
Prompt to Plan a Surprise Weekend TripPlan a surprise trip for me this weekend starting from [my location].
I don’t want to choose the destination myself.
My preferences:
- Maximum travel time: [X hours]
- Budget: [budget]
- Trip duration: [one day/two days]
- Transport: [car/bike/train/bus/public transport]
- I like: [nature/beaches/mountains/waterfalls/food/history/road trips/etc.]
- I want to avoid: [crowds/long drives/hot weather/etc.]
Suggest 5 destinations that match these preferences.
For each destination, tell me:

Then pick ONE destination as your best recommendation and create a complete itinerary for the trip in chronological order.
Also give me one backup destination in case weather, traffic, or availability makes the first option unsuitable.
Compare Travel Options, Distances, and Travel Times
There are situations where you prefer multiple transport options for visiting a specific place, or you want the shortest and most reliable option for transport.
This is where Ask Maps’ features can help you. If you are planning to visit a specific place, instead of switching between multiple transport types, such as walking, driving, and public transit, and checking how much time each would take, you can simply ask Google Maps to provide all the transport options to that location in a comparison table.
For example, I live in Yanam, and if I want to go to my nearest city, Kakinada, I can ask Google Maps to show all the transport options available, how much distance each transport covers, and how much time it will take.
And the Ask Maps feature calculates all the distances, analyzes them, and creates a detailed table for you comparing each transport option and how reliable they are. Plus, you can personalize it with other additional details such as whether the transport is available for the location you want to visit or not.
Prompt to Compare All Travel OptionsI need to travel from [starting location] to [destination].
Compare every practical transport option available for this journey, including driving, bike, walking, public transport, buses, trains, metro, taxis, and any other realistic option available in this area.

If public transport is available, explain the journey step by step, including where I need to board, change services, and get off.

Ask Maps Is the AI Feature Google Maps Actually Needed
Google Ask Maps is a game changer if you use it in the right way. Plus, there are very generous limits; most of this AI feature is available even for the free tier, which allows you to plan the best trips and even use it to create a surprise trip for your weekend.
Plus, you can get informed about everything regarding a place before you even visit, so that you can be prepared for all outcomes.

The inside story of how Trabzonspor pulled off Salah deal
- Published
As Mohamed Salah signed his two-year deal in front of tens of thousands of fans inside Trabzonspor's Papara Park stadium, the man putting his signature to the contract next to the Egyptian was struggling to keep the smile off his face.
The reaction of supporters over the previous few days had already convinced club president Ertugrul Dogan he had pulled off a transfer coup.
"He's the biggest Muslim footballer in the world. He's an influential role model," he told BBC Sport Africa and BBC Turkish.
"We held Salah's signing ceremony in front of 35,000 people.
"It was clear from everything he did that he felt that love, and he told us as much too. He thanked us."
So how did Dogan persuade one of football's megastars to join a club without Champions League football and which has won the Turkish title only once since its heyday in the 1970s and early 1980s?
'Why should I choose Trabzonspor?'
Located on the Black Sea coast, the city of Trabzon sits near the border with Georgia in the north-east corner of Turkey.
With a population of around 800,000 people, it is not even in the top 20 when it comes to the country's largest urban centres.
But Dogan claims it has something special.
"I always say this about Trabzonspor and the city - we're the biggest one-club city in the world.
"Salah asked us something like, 'Why should I choose Trabzonspor now?'
"We told him about the city and said: 'You can be sure you will meet a group of supporters unlike any you have experienced before. You'll feel the genuine love those people have inside them'."
Born in January 1977, Dogan is himself a son of Trabzon.
The businessman made his money through a series of different ventures, including real estate and hazelnuts, before moving into the energy sector and specialising in biofuels.
He became Trabzonspor president in 2023, shortly after the club's most successful season in recent memory - having won the league title in 2021-22.
Under Dogan's watch, the Black Sea Storm, as the club is known, have finished third, seventh and third in the Super Lig.
Last season they won the Turkish Cup under coach Fatih Tekke, who is now looking to guide his team into the Europa League, despite a 1-0 home defeat in the first leg of their play-off tie against Hungary's Ferencvaros.
"We are working to make Trabzonspor and Trabzon itself a destination for talented young players from all over the world," said Dogan.
"We want to take them to the next level, to move on to bigger European clubs. Those young players… [combined with] star players… a star in every way, with their lifestyle, their professionalism, their smile, their positive energy.
"Mohamed Salah is a really great example in this respect."
- Who replaces Salah as Africa's Premier League king? 
  - Published1 day ago
- Why has Salah chosen to join Trabzonspor? 
  - Published6 August
Attention 'cannot be given financial value'
During the off-season, Trabzonspor sold 20-year-old Ivorian midfielder Christ Inao Oulai to Fiorentina and Brazilian forward Felipe Augusto, 22, to Zenit St Petersburg - both for large profits after only one season at the club.
Young players from Albania, Belgium, Cape Verde and Portugal have arrived to replace them, but Dogan wants to continue balancing those talents with experienced names.
Cameroon goalkeeper Andre Onana has returned for a second season on loan from Manchester United, but the deal for Salah is the potential gamechanger.
"The attention it has generated and the level of engagement it has created around the world cannot easily be given a direct financial value," explained Dogan, who has openly admitted that Salah will be earning €17m per year (£14.6m, $19.9m), as well as 20% of any merchandise with his name on.
"Purely from a financial perspective, this transfer has no direct return as such.
"We put up our season tickets this year. We had to make another increase. I told our fans, 'Look, I'm bringing you Salah, one of the biggest stars in the world'."
Dogan says nearly 70% of Salah's salary this year was covered by season ticket sales made within the first four or five days after the announcement of his arrival.
The initial target was 25,000 season ticket sales, but the club now expects to exceed 30,000, while major companies have been calling the president, looking to get involved in Salah-mania.
"We're having important discussions in Turkey, Europe and the Arab world as well."
'The whole city lives for football'
The news that Trabzonspor had won the race for Salah's signature after nine stellar seasons at Liverpool raised a few eyebrows.
Many had expected the man who sits fourth on the all-time list of Premier League goalscorers to sign a huge contract with a club in the Saudi Pro League like Cristiano Ronaldo or join Lionel Messi in the United States.
But while there was competition, Dogan says the deal happened quickly once negotiations really got going.
"Once we started talking, both sides genuinely approached each other very sincerely," he said.
"We'd actually been pursuing him since the World Cup, but we knew at the start he was also talking to other clubs."
This meant Trabzonspor initially had to bide their time, given Dogan says there is an unwritten rule in Turkey that if one club is holding talks then the others will wait.
"Yes, there were clubs in Turkey who were interested," he confirmed.
"After they said, 'We've pulled out of this transfer', we started talks. I think it took about five or six days to conclude.
"We had the first meeting over Zoom. At that point it was really just the two sides getting to know each other. Then Salah was on holiday - he was in Mykonos - and after that the talks continued again via Zoom."
Trabzonspor finally brought Salah to Turkey for his medical in Istanbul.
Dogan says they decided to hold it there to show the 34-year-old the kind of reception he would get across Turkey, not just in Trabzon.
Thousands of fans were at the airport to greet Salah when he arrived, even though it was in the middle of a working day.
Trabzonspor's new star also made his debut in Istanbul, entering the fray as a second-half substitute in a 1-1 draw against Kasimpasa on the opening day of the new league season last weekend.
He is expected to make his home league debut in Trabzon on Sunday.
"The whole city lives for football," said Dogan.
"Everywhere you go, on every corner, the city gives that player that energy and that happiness."
Thanks to Mohamed Salah, Trabzonspor's president could be smiling for a while yet.

'High risk' of lake bursting and causing second flood, warns China
- Published
China has warned there is a "high risk" that a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may burst, causing a second flood downstream.
The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river.
As of Friday morning, an estimated 2.5 million cubic metres of water had accumulated at the barrier lake, according to state broadcaster CCTV. A barrier lake is a body of water formed when debris dams up a river.
Officials said that three million cubic metres of water is expected to flow into the lake between Thursday and Saturday, posing a "high risk of breach".
The barrier lake, which formed at the confluence of the Chhochen Khola and Purepu Tsangpo rivers, has already started to overflow, according to China's Ministry of Water Resources. The area has also seen heavy rain.
Authorities have sent engineering teams to monitor the lake's water levels and the atmospheric conditions.
A CCTV report on Friday morning said that most of the Chinese emergency services were stuck at a village about 7km (4 miles) from Gyirong Port, the major land crossing linking Nepal and China which was hit by Wednesday's massive flood.
This was because the barrier lake was "overflowing non-stop" which could lead to fresh floods or debris flows.
Due to the risks, search and rescue operations had to be suspended near the Nepal-Tibet border, according to the report.

The lake is in the same region as the Langtang Lirung peak, where the collapsed glacier is believed to have originated, and several kilometres upstream from Gyirong Port.
Separately, Nepali authorities have warned of the risk of blockages causing further floods along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers.
They have warned people to stay away from the rivers until further notice.
Scientists have said that the flood on Wednesday was likely to have been caused by part of a glacier near Langtang Lirung collapsing into the river below, which in turn caused a massive surge downstream carrying water and debris.
Several hundred people have died in Nepal and with hundreds more still missing after the flash flood. On the Tibet side of the border alone, more than 550 are missing - nearly half of which are foreigners.

With a seemingly never-ending pool of options, it can be hard to know if you're picking the best bar for a happy hour or night out.
Take it from Stephanie Ridgway, who worked at several bars and distilleries before becoming the director of brand advocacy for the liquor brand Charles Jacquin et Cie.
"I've been in my fair share of bars, from dives to high-end cocktail lounges," Ridgway told Business Insider. "I've developed a keen eye for what sets the good apart from the great — and behaviors that will always raise a red flag for me."
To help spare you a bad experience, Ridgway shared her top red flags to look out for at a bar so you know when it may be best to beeline toward the exit.
It's never a good sign when a bar is dirty, especially if it's not busy
Ridgway's alarm bells start going off the second she walks into a dirty bar. For her, that includes things like a sticky bar tops, soiled towels on counters, and dirty glassware.
"Everything else about the place becomes suspect to me and indicates to me that the bar staff doesn't take pride in their workplace," she said.
She's "exponentially" more concerned if the bar isn't busy.
It's important to give bartenders some grace if you're heading out on a Friday or Saturday night when it might be busier than normal, she added.
However, if you randomly pop in during the middle of the day and there's a sticky countertop and dirty glasses, you're perhaps better off going somewhere else.
After all, she said, a familiar mantra for everyone in the industry is, "Time to lean is time to clean." Tidying up during slow periods is key to a well-kept bar.
A quality bar should limit the use of batched cocktails
Ridgway said that it's smart for bars to have some of their highest-selling cocktails batched and ready to pour. But handing guests a drink from a large premade jug can still detract from the overall experience if it's overdone.
"When I sit down at a bar and order a cocktail, I want to be treated to the full visual effect that watching the bartender carefully crafting my drink provides," she told BI. "In short, I came here, in part, for the show."
A truly great bar knows that offering great service and a special experience can matter as much as how delicious a drink tastes.
Intoxicated employees are a big no-no
If you walk into a bar and notice the bartender seems to have had one too many drinks themselves, swing the door the other way. Just because they work around spirits doesn't give them a free pass to get drunk on the clock.
Ridgway said it's common for a bartender to join regulars for a sip of something boozy throughout the night, but there are professional limits.
"I don't go to a bar to have someone not fully in control of their faculties mix me a drink," she told BI.
A dismissive bartender is also a tough sell for Ridgway
When you go out to a bar, you're handing over some of your hard-earned dollars for the beverage of your choice.
Ridgway said it's perfectly reasonable to expect that mutual transaction to occur "sans bad attitude."
"When I see bartenders rolling their eyes or exhibiting some other sort of dismissive behavior upon hearing a drink order, I'm pretty sure I'm never coming back," she said.
Pay attention to the quality of the spirits behind the bar
If you're headed to a craft cocktail bar or a spot marketed as higher-end, you may want to take a close look at the liquor shelves.
Ridgway knows better than most that liquor can be expensive, and bars need to control costs somewhere. However, being financially savvy isn't an excuse to stock shelves with the cheapest, lowest-quality spirits.
"Bar managers and beverage directors have, quite literally, hundreds of quality brands at their disposal and, with a little research, can find some delicious, well-made, cost-effective alternatives with which to stock their bars," Ridgway said.
She said if she sees a bartender using poor-quality gin to "craft" a martini, she'll probably pass on it.
This story was originally published on July 31, 2024, and most recently updated on August 28, 2026.

The chess calendar is crowded. Top players rarely get to take a breather these days with so many big events, across formats, taking place across the globe.
And it is going to get even more crowded with the newly launched Total World Chess Championship Tour. Its pilot will be held at Budapest from November 10 to 21. Lined up for the event are many of the biggest names in chess, headlined by World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen.
There are three Indians in the fray — Arjun Erigaisi and the Chennai siblings R. Praggnanandhaa and R. Vaishali. Arjun is one of the eight top 10 players that will compete in Budapest.
The presence of men like Fabiano Caruanan (World No. 2), Vincent Keymer (No. 5) and Wesley So (No. 6) ensures it would be a stiffly contested event, which will feature 24 players in all.
The first full tour will begin next year with four legs to be played in cities across the world. Conceived by Norway Chess, with blessings from the world chess governing body FIDE, the new tour combines different formats of chess — classical, rapid and blitz.
There are, of course, separate World championships for all those categories, and the classical format Total World Chess Championship is not quite classical in fact: the time control is 45 minutes with an increment of 30 seconds per move.
That may look more rapid than classical, for which the time control is usually 90 minutes for the first 40 moves and then 30 minutes for the rest of the game with increment.
Total Chess, to be fair, isn’t calling its format classical, but fast classical. That makes sense. For, classical chess needs to retain its prime place.
It is still the World champions in classical chess — be it Bobby Fischer, Garry Kasparov or Viswanathan Anand — that the world will always remember vividly.
The Total Chess Championship Tour, though, is a welcome addition to the mind sport. The more the merrier.

Republican campaign committees want the Supreme Court to mandate lower prices for election commercials on broadcast TV stations. If the court agrees, broadcasters would be forced to offer their lowest ad prices to political parties and joint fundraising committees.
For a more thorough description of the legal issues in the dispute, see this article that Ars published yesterday. In short, US law requires broadcasters to offer individual candidates the “lowest unit charge,” or LUC, during the 60 days before an election. The law helps level the playing field somewhat by letting candidates make their cases to voters who watch broadcast TV without needing to raise exorbitant sums of money.
The Trump administration, acting through the Federal Communications Commission, ordered broadcast TV stations to also give these discounts to political parties and joint fundraising committees, which face fewer limits on how much money they can raise and spend. Four Democratic candidates appealed, and a judges’ panel at the US Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit ruled that the FCC order cannot be enforced because it contradicts the plain language of US law.
The National Republican Congressional Committee and National Republican Senatorial Committee, which intervened in the case to support the FCC’s position, told the 4th Circuit court yesterday that they intend to appeal to the Supreme Court.
GOP seeks quick rulings
The committees submitted an emergency motion for a stay and asked the 4th Circuit to rule on that motion immediately so they can file a petition to the Supreme Court. “Intervenors respectfully request that the Court rule on this stay motion as soon as possible—whether by expediting or waiving response briefs—to permit Intervenors to seek emergency relief at the Supreme Court,” Republican committees told the court.
The court responded quickly, issuing an order today to deny the Republican committee’s motion and to immediately issue a mandate that can be appealed to the Supreme Court. Republicans will now seek swift action from the Supreme Court in an attempt to overturn the 4th Circuit ruling before the 60-day discount period starts on September 4.

A study across the various units of a premier eye care hospital in southern India has found that using advanced air filters in operation theatres offers no added benefit to infection prevention in cataract surgery. The study, Comparison of Cataract Surgery Endophthalmitis Rates in Operating Rooms with and without Laminar Air Flow and HEPA Filters, authored by Sheena Song, David F. Chang et al., was published in the American Journal of Ophthalmology in August.
Aravind Eye Care System (AECS), which has a network of 14 regional hospitals in south India, performs around 50% to 60% of cataract surgeries on indigent patients at little or no cost to the patients.
AECS system has operating rooms of varying types depending on the hospital location and its age. Since the hospital has standardised surgical protocols, antibiotic prophylaxis, instrument processing and environmental safety across its units, it decided to examine if installation of laminar air flow (LAF) and high efficiency particulate air filters would reduce the rates of postoperative endophthalmitis (POE).
POE is a complication that can occur after cataract surgery. Infection is mainly due to invasion of the globe by microbial flora, bacteria, or fungi from the adnexa (structures surround and support the eye ball) and environment during the surgery If not treated promptly, it could lead to vision loss.
The study
Researchers at ACES conducted a retrospective study of the 4,52,770 cataract surgeries performed at its 14 hospitals in India in 2023.
“The retrospective analysis reviewed the cataract surgeries, all performed using identical surgical and infection-control protocols, including periocular povidone-iodine and intracameral moxifloxacin. Surgeries were performed in operating rooms with varying air-handling units: LAF with HEPA, central AC with HEPA, central AC without HEPA, and split AC without HEPA,” explained R. Venkatesh, chief medical officer at Aravind Eye Care Hospital in Puducherry and one of the authors of the study.
The multicentre, retrospective study, found that using LAF or HEPA filtration for cataract surgery offered no infection reducing benefit.
Also Read: Insurance can better cataract surgery outcomes for India’s elderly: study
Across all groups, the overall POE rate was extremely low at 0.016%, with no statistically significant differences between the different ventilation systems—even when analysed separately by surgical method: phacoemulsification vs manual small incision cataract surgery MSICS or patient category: paying vs non-paying, the researchers said.
“This contradicts mandating these more expensive air handling unit systems for ophthalmic surgery. Recommending or requiring LAF or HEPA unnecessarily imposes additional infrastructural barriers for ophthalmic operating rooms in resource-limited settings and for office-based surgery in high-income countries,” the study concluded.
Towards safe surgeries
The study noted that the results of the analysis showed that safe cataract surgery is achievable without an expensive LAF or HEPA system, provided rigid aseptic protocols are followed.
“This could remove unnecessary infrastructure barriers in resource-limited settings and make cataract surgery more accessible across all types of surgical facilities worldwide,” said Dr. Venkatesh.
A similar result came up in an earlier study conducted nearly a decade ago. That study was conducted by Shalinder Sabherwal of the Department of Community Ophthalmology and Public Health Research at Dr. Shroff’s Charity Eye Hospital, New Delhi.
Dr. Sabherwal, Deepali Chaku et al. had published their findings in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology in May 2020, based on their analysis of surgery outcomes for five years between 2013 and 2018. The study, published as the article Are high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters and laminar flow necessary in operating rooms to control acute post-operative endophthalmitis? relied on a retrospective analysis of medical records of 88,297 cataract surgeries conducted in a single network of a tertiary and four secondary hospitals across north India. It identified cases of endophthalmitis from the records between January 2013 and June 2018.
The analysis found that the incidence at secondary centres, without LAF and HEPA filters, were comparable to that found in the tertiary centres with these facilities.

Fintech unicorn Raise Financial Services has roped in former Upstox executive Abhishek Singh as the chief executive officer (CEO) of its new insurtech vertical Pluto Insurance. Singh confirmed the development in a post on LinkedIn. His bio on the networking platform also reflected the new designation. “Twenty-three years in this industry, and I am as excited as I was on day one. Happy to announce that I am joining Pluto Insurance… I've spent most of my career wanting to build things that solve real problems for real people, not just move numbers on a board. Pluto Insurance gives me that shot, at scale, in a category that badly needs it,” said Singh. In his post, Singh added that Pluto plans to build a platform for “what the customer actually needs, backed by cutting edge tech and AI”. An alumnus of ICFAI Business School, Singh counts more than two decades of experience under his belt. He previously served at companies like Aviva India, PNB Metlife and Edelweiss Tokio Life Insurance. He was last working as a senior director at Upstox, according to his LinkedIn profile. While the website of the new platform is yet to go live, it is already inviting users to join its waitlist. As per its website, Pluto Insurance will be housed under GreenLife Insurance Broking Pvt Ltd (GIBL), and bears the same IRDAI registration number and licence code as GIBL. The appointment comes three months after Raise Financial acquired GIBL in an undisclosed cash-and-stock deal. At the time, the fintech unicorn had said that it would invest $15 Mn in GIBL to build a direct consumer insurance distribution platform. Notably, recent reports also suggested that GIBL has been rebranded to Pluto Insurance. However, Raise Financial has made no public announcement of the same. Notably, Singh is the second senior executive onboarded by the company in the past two months. In late-July, Ranjeet Walunj said that he had joined Pluto Insurance as its chief product and technology officer (CPTO). While there appears no clarity on what Pluto Insurance exactly does, Walunj earlier said that the platform would streamline insurance for consumers. “At Pluto, we aim to build this (insurance) business differently: spam-free, easy-to-use, product-tech led, enabled with AI and most importantly, a platform that puts consumers and their needs first!” Walunj said then. Nevertheless, Pluto Insurance will look to leverage GIBL’s strong presence in the B2B insurance distributor space and its offline network spanning over 50 cities and towns. Founded in 2021 by former Paytm Money CEO Pravin Jadhav, Alok Pandey, Jay Prakash Gupta, and Raunak Rathi, Raise Financial is a unicorn that operates a gamut of fintech platforms. Besides stock broking platform Dhan, Raise also owns and operates financial market information platform Upsurge, market research platform ScanX, and AI-driven trading insights platform FuzzAI. It also acquired new-age media startup Filter Coffee last year. The Indian Medical Association (IMA) on Wednesday (August 26, 2026) issued a public health advisory on the seasonal surge in Influenza A (H1N1), or swine flu, during the monsoon, urging people not to self-medicate with antibiotics and antivirals and advising immediate medical attention in case of severe symptoms.
The IMA said India is witnessing a seasonal increase in H1N1 cases, with metropolitan centres such as Delhi recording more than 1,770 laboratory-confirmed cases, alongside cases reported in Maharashtra, Karnataka and West Bengal.
The advisory said surveillance by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has confirmed that the circulating virus remains seasonal Influenza A (H1N1), with no novel genetic mutations detected.
“India is witnessing a seasonal surge in Influenza A (H1N1) / Swine Flu cases during the monsoon period,” the IMA said, adding that while heightened vigilance is necessary, “there is no cause for panic”.
The medical body said the majority of H1N1 infections are mild and self-limiting.
According to the advisory, H1N1 typically presents with sudden onset of high-grade fever and chills, persistent dry cough and sore throat, severe muscle aches and fatigue, headache, runny or congested nose, and, more frequently in children, nausea, vomiting or loose stools.
The IMA stressed that Influenza A (H1N1) is a viral illness and antibiotics do not kill viruses.
“Do not consume Azithromycin, Amoxicillin-Clavulanate, Cefixime, or other antibiotics for flu symptoms,” it said, warning that indiscriminate antibiotic use during viral surges can destroy protective microbiome flora and fuel lethal Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR).
The IMA clarified that antibiotics should be used only when a qualified physician diagnoses a secondary bacterial infection based on clinical and laboratory findings.
On antiviral medication, the advisory said Oseltamivir is a prescription-only drug and should be used only for specific clinical categories under medical supervision.
“Do not self-administer antivirals,” the IMA said.
The medical body also listed several warning signs requiring immediate emergency medical attention, including difficulty in breathing, shortness of breath or rapid breathing, chest pain or persistent pressure, and bluish discolouration of the lips or fingers.
Patients experiencing coughing up blood, drowsiness, confusion, extreme sleepiness or seizures, persistent vomiting and inability to tolerate oral fluids should also seek emergency care, it said.
For children, inability to feed, lethargy, grunting or severe chest retractions have been listed as red-flag symptoms requiring urgent medical attention.
The IMA advised people to follow preventive measures, including frequent handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds or using an alcohol-based hand sanitiser.
It also recommended covering the mouth and nose with a tissue or bent elbow while coughing or sneezing and wearing a well-fitted mask in crowded and enclosed spaces.
“Stay Home When Sick: Avoid schools, workplaces, and social gatherings for at least 24 hours after fever has resolved without fever-reducing medications,” the advisory said.
The IMA also strongly advised annual seasonal influenza vaccination for healthcare personnel, pregnant women, the elderly and people with underlying chronic medical conditions.

'Ghana was the crime scene': The country leading the demand for slavery reparations
- Published
This year has seen a dramatic change in tone in the global conversation about the transatlantic slave trade.
The demand for formal apologies, debt relief and financial compensation from nations and institutions that benefited from slavery has become increasingly forceful.
In March, a resolution was passed at the United Nations recognising slavery as "the greatest crime against humanity" - though the United States voted against the resolution and every European nation abstained from the vote.
The UK, which alongside Portugal dominated the transatlantic slave trade, has consistently rejected the idea of paying reparations, which is perhaps unsurprising given estimates of what Britain "owes" in damages to nations affected run into many trillions of pounds.
This resistance has not deterred the country that has become the leading voice on reparations: Ghana.
Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable"
It was Ghana that tabled the UN resolution, and in June, a summit on reparations was held in its capital, Accra, with delegates from around 80 countries, who concluded that recompense was long overdue.
"Ghana has always been a pan-African leader. We're the first country to attain independence in sub-Saharan Africa and to prove that it is possible to fight imperial might, and win," Foreign Minister Samuel Okuzeto Ablakwa tells me.
Ghana has been given special responsibility by the African Union to be "champion for reparatory justice" and it is clearly a role the country's political leadership is taking seriously.
In part that is because about 10-15% of the estimated 12 million Africans who were forcibly removed from their homes, torn from their villages, and dehumanised on a scale never before seen, were from what is now Ghana. Even more were shipped from its shores.
"Ghana was the crime scene where these atrocities took place, so Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable," Ablakwa says.
The minister has called for a system of reparatory justice that funds educational grants, venture capital for young African entrepreneurs and research into enduring health issues that some argue may trace their roots back to the severe malnutrition and inhumane conditions of enslavement.
And though he insists that this is not about direct financial gain for African leaders, one of the demands laid out at the recent summit on reparations clearly talked of debt relief and debt cancellation.
He also wants individual institutions that benefited from the slave trade to be held accountable and pay compensation. Among these is the Church of England.
In the 18th Century, the Church's missionary wing ran plantations and owned hundreds of slaves, which helped fund its work across the Americas and beyond.
Many Church of England clergy independently owned slaves, and a recent report by the Church's endowment fund reported the institution made large investments in the slave trade from which it made huge sums of money.
In July, the leader of the Church, the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally, visited Ghana in one of her first international visits in the role.
She travelled to Cape Coast Castle, one of the many coastal fortresses that had been run by the British, and where enslaved people were held before enduring the brutal "Middle Passage" to the Americas.
As she toured the dungeons where slaves were held and walked through "the door of no return" through which they were forced before being loaded on to ships, Dame Sarah looked emotional and stopped to pray.
"I felt the weight of the depth of evil that the transatlantic slave trade was. You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in," the Archbishop said.
She also prayed in a 17th Century chapel that was positioned directly above the dungeons.
"For me that is such a stark illustration of the way the Church was involved in the slave trade," she says. "How can the church have sat above the horrors that were going on below?".
"The Church of England has apologised for the part that we played in the transatlantic slave trade but we've also said there needs to be action that relates to that," Archbishop Sarah said.
The Church has set up a £100m ($135m) social impact fund designed to benefit communities thought to continue to feel the enduring legacy of the slave trade today.
But within the Church, the establishment of the fund has encountered resistance, just as the global push for nations to pay reparations has done.
One of the key counter-arguments centres on the fact that some Africans were themselves complicit in the capture and sale of their fellow people.
But Foreign Minister Ablakwa emphatically rejects this narrative. "I think that there's a strategy to divide and conquer and to create a very contrived confusion," he argues.
He stresses that the entire architecture of chattel enslavement was curated by Western slave-owning powers, who simply utilised local actors to help carry out their plans.
The foreign minister points out that when the laws, insurance policies, and financial architectures of the trade were being drafted, "there was no African at the table".
"We denounce and totally reject those claims that Africans are as guilty and complicit as those who masterminded this whole atrocity," he says.
Yet, within Ghana itself, the conversation around African complicity is far more nuanced, and for some traditional leaders, acknowledging the past is a vital prerequisite part of healing.
King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, the Ga Mantse, leader of Ghana's Ga people, recently took the step of publicly apologising for his ancestors' involvement in the slave trade.
"I think that the transatlantic slave trade was the greatest crime against humanity, and ancestors also took part as players in that trade," says the king.
The Ga people became middlemen who traded with Europeans. They sold gold, ivory and ultimately enslaved Africans, often those captured in local conflicts, in exchange for the manufactured goods brought mainly by the British and Dutch, including textiles, alcohol and guns.
But the king felt he needed to say sorry not just for his own people's complicity, but the complicity of other Africans too.
"I stand on the same point of apologising on behalf of all traditional authorities and my ancestors and forebears for the part they also played in the slavery of our brothers and sisters.
"It has affected lives and societies up to now, and to be able to go forward, you have to look at your past. It dawns on us to admit our fault and correct it," he says.
The king believes strongly in the need for those who benefited from the slave trade to pay reparations and acknowledges that he, too, needs to commit to making financial amends.
"I believe that it underpins a state of moral courage and credibility."
For the Ga Mantse, admitting fault does not dilute the guilt of European empires; rather, it solidifies Africa's moral standing and sets an example as to how to move forward.
But Ghana is leading the way in another aspect of trying to heal the damage done by the slave trade. The country has run a high-profile campaign inviting the African diaspora - particularly African-Americans - to visit the continent.
It has been promoted as a means of bringing people together in the shared story of their traumatic past, with "reparations" quite literally focussing on "repair" at a very human level.
Yaw Asare, now a Ghanaian PhD student at Howard University, previously worked within the President of Ghana's Diaspora Office, which ran the campaign.
Initially, the gathering of black people from across the globe was, he felt, "a beautiful, profound experience devoid of capitalist motives". But he says in some respects the initiative soon morphed.
"The Ghana Tourism Authority also latched on to it and then used it to enhance their tourism project," Asare explains, saying the initiative started to become less about "repair" and more about hitting tourism quotas.
Asare says the campaign has often viewed the returning diaspora simply as a means of foreign cash flow, raising prices and negatively altering local economies.
"Now (local) people are finding that they cannot afford basic things," Asare says, describing how local Ghanaians were economically sidelined.
More devastatingly, he feels the commercialisation of the initiative overshadowed the deep, psychological work that is desperately needed for locals as well as "returning" members of the diaspora.
"We are dealing with humans, we are dealing with people. We cannot reduce them to, 'come see this site, pay this entrance fee'," Asare says.
He also questions - in an initiative that was partly supposed to be about addressing the trauma of Africans in the diaspora - why they were required to pay entrance fees at the same rates as European tourists at, for example, the coastal castles where slaves were trafficked.
He says all of this means a missed opportunity to address deep-rooted trauma some of which he feels is etched into the very geography and psychology of modern Ghana.
"Go to Jamestown (in Accra), people are huddled together because there is the fear of 'if I live far away, I could be taken'," Asare says, pointing to how centuries-old concerns dictated why people built their houses so closely together.
Jamestown is one of the oldest districts in the city, a community originally built around a British coastal fort where slaves were brought, traded and then sent on ships to the Americas.
For Asare, true reparatory justice must prioritise human connection and healing over financial transactions.
"We have to remove the band-aid and then look at the sore, the gaping wound that's present," Asare says about what he sees as real "reparations". "And see how we can dress it and nurse it and heal".

In August 2026, after the retailer Target removed a costume from its website that faced backlash for evoking racist minstrel and blackface imagery, a video circulated online that social media users claimed (archived) showed an ad that Target also pulled featuring the costume in question.
The video showed an animated character wearing the since-removed costume advertising various $5 fall deals.
One Threads user who shared the video wrote, "Target pulls national ad campaign after accusations that new spokesperson is 'racist.'" "Spokesperson" appeared to refer to the character in the video.
The alleged ad also circulated on Facebook (archived) and X (archived), where community notes identified it as a product of artificial intelligence.
The video was fake. It came from an X account that described its content as "probably AI" and marked (archived) the video itself "Made with AI" on its timeline.
Aside from the creator's own admission that they used AI to create the video, it also contained obvious signs of fakery. There were multiple instances of incorrect or unreadable text throughout the video, a classic sign of the use of AI.
For example, at 0:01, on-screen text read "HEYY TURGET FANS." It was unlikely Target would misspell its own name in public advertising. At 0:02, the costumed character held a candle that contained misshapen letters in the word "Pumpkin." At 0:05, three products appeared on screen, one of which featured totally unreadable text.
(@JasonRink, accessed via X, illustrated by Snopes)
The widely criticized costume itself was real. Target announced (archived) on Aug. 24, 2026, that it had "pulled an offensive Halloween costume that should never have been part of our assortment."
The retailer's statement continued:
As a company, we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry. We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won't happen again.
Critics of the costume said it evoked racist minstrel and blackface imagery. Blackface minstrelsy — performances where white performers artificially darkened their faces and depicted Black people as "lazy, ignorant, superstitious, hypersexual, and prone to thievery and cowardice," according to the National Museum of African American History and Culture — are widely considered racist today.
Social media users criticized aspects of the costume such as its large, caricatured mouth and the model's pose, which was similar to images of Jim Crow, a blackface minstrelsy character whose name later became associated with racial segregation laws in the U.S.
For further reading, Snopes routinely investigates AI-generated content.

Jalgaon, August 28, 2026: In a significant breakthrough against organised financial fraud, the cyber police have unearthed a multi-state cybercrime network and arrested a key operative involved in managing "mule" bank accounts.
The syndicate is alleged to have laundered over Rs 2.15 crore obtained through various online baits, including fraudulent investment schemes, fake part-time job offers and "digital arrest" scams.
Investigation Traces Suspicious Accounts
According to the police, the investigation began in August 2026 after local residents from Jalgaon approached the cyber police to inquire about freezes placed on their accounts at three different banks.
Upon verifying the accounts through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCCRP) and the SAMANVAY portal of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), investigators found that the accounts were flagged for suspicious activity across several states.
The account holders revealed they had been persuaded to provide their banking credentials to an acquaintance, identified as K.B. Sankhala, under the impression that the accounts would be used for a legitimate tours and travels business.
Following this lead, the cyber police questioned Sankhala, a 31-year-old resident of Jalgaon originally from Nagaur, Rajasthan.
During interrogation, Sankhala reportedly confessed to luring individuals into opening current accounts, which he then handed over to a Mumbai-based associate identified only as Tony. For every account delivered, Sankhala allegedly received a commission of Rs 40,000.
Money Trail Reveals Rs 2.14 Crore
A detailed analysis of the money trail conducted by Maharashtra Cyber Mumbai revealed that between July 2024 and early 2025, approximately Rs 2.14 crore was funnelled through various accounts.
The fraudulent funds were typically withdrawn via ATMs and cheques or transferred through a complex web of beneficiary accounts to obscure the source of the money.

Mastermind Still Being Traced
Sankhala has been arrested for his role in the conspiracy and for being a member of an organised cybercrime gang. Authorities are now working to identify the Mumbai-based mastermind and other field agents active across the country.
Police have urged citizens to remain vigilant and never share their bank account details or OTPs with others, even if they claim it is for business purposes.

4 men plead guilty to torching 4 London-based ambulances operated by Jewish charity
Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack in north London earlier this year that many said was a direct result of the start of the Iran war
LONDON -- Four men pleaded guilty Friday to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack in north London earlier this year that many said was a direct result of the start of the Iran war.
Sentencing will take place in the spring of 2027 at the conclusion of a separate trial involving another man charged in connection with the ambulance attack, Justice Bobbie Cheema-Grubb said at London’s Central Criminal Court.
Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both 18, faced a charge of destroying or damaging property and of being reckless as to whether life would be endangered.
The four ambulances torched in the early hours of March 23 were owned by Hatzola, a Jewish volunteer-led charity operating in the Golders Green area of north London. The ambulances each cost around 250,000 pounds ($340,000).
The attack was one of several incidents deemed to have been antisemitic that took place in the weeks after the U.S. and Israel first launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.
Three of the defendants were said to have set fire to the fully stocked vehicles, while a fourth waited in a car. The resulting blaze caused gas canisters inside the ambulances to explode, and nearby apartments and a synagogue were also damaged by the fire.
Prosecutor Leo Seelig suggested the incident had a “terrorist connection” although no mention was made in court of potential proxies working for Iran.
Counterterrorism police had looked into the possible involvement of Iranian proxies in the Jewish ambulance arson, as well as other attacks on Jewish sites in London.
Most have been claimed online by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right.
The Iranian Embassy in the U.K. has said that it “categorically rejects” allegations of involvement in “violent activities or incidents in the United Kingdom.”
At the same hearing, a fifth defendant, Subhan Ahmed, 18, pleaded not guilty to a charge of assisting an offender. Ahmed, who is alleged to have helped to get rid of the car used in the attack, will go on trial on Jan. 27.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".

The heartbreak of reporting from a camp housing Nepal flood survivors
- Published
I enter the camp to an absolutely heartbreaking scene.
Hundreds of people are queuing outside, desperately trying to see if they can find their loved ones.
This army camp in Nuwakot, one of the main districts in central Nepal affected by devastating flash floods and massive landslides, has been turned into a search-and-rescue centre.
Inside, a woman cradling an infant in her arms is crying hysterically. Her entire family, including her father, husband and mother, are all missing. She is traumatised, and in so much pain.
There are other people who have sustained injuries, and some who say they had miraculously survived.
One driver who was working in Rasuwa tells us he'd been thrown into the water when the floods hit. He still doesn't know how he managed to survive. Yet while thankful to be alive, he is also devastated - he's also lost more than 20 of his friends.
When I try speaking to him he is unable to focus, and not in a proper state of mind. There are tears in his eyes.
At one point while filming, a woman - perhaps in her 60s or 70s - is taken out of a helicopter and brought to the centre to be treated.
She suddenly collapses. I later learn she has died. It is tremendously difficult to describe what I witnessed.
Every hour at the camp there are dozens of helicopters coming and going, and many people are receiving treatment.
Whenever these helicopters come, people look at them with a ray of hope their loved ones will be inside.
Even as the helicopters land, blowing gusts of wind and mud down on everyone, people still don't look away - trying to catch a glimpse of who's on board.
After we leave the camp we try to get access to the internet so we can share what we've seen, but internet connectivity is extremely poor, so we drive about three hours back to our office in Kathmandu.
Disasters are something I have covered several times in Nepal, but this is one of the most harrowing I have ever seen.
But as a journalist you do your job: you receive information and report what you see.

In a climate that mixes extreme political turbulence with an unprecedented age of misinformation, each year it grows exceedingly difficult to determine whether what you are seeing online is not only authentic but presented in the correct context.
Both critics and supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration have been guilty of spreading photos or videos that are either purposefully or mistakenly miscaptioned, usually in an attempt to underline a point that aligns with their political beliefs.
For instance, Snopes has investigated everything from liberal-leaning claims that a Fox News reporter deliberately misrepresented the color of the green, algae-infested water of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to conservative-leaning claims that a Craigslist ad was used to hire protestors to speak out against Trump. Both the video and the image were miscaptioned and spread online in contexts that were not based in reality.
There has been no shortage of such images and videos circulating during Trump's second term, so we've dug into the Snopes archives for media related to Trump and his administration we ultimately determined to be miscaptioned.

Just as new data centers face growing backlash from neighboring communities, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is about to make it harder for people to weigh in on any pollution those centers create.
Trump’s EPA wants to let data centers hide their air pollution
The Trump administration wants to scrap another federal air pollution rule. Advocates say it’ll help data center developers avoid public scrutiny.
The EPA plans to toss out a federal rule requiring public notice and an opportunity to comment when certain industrial sites apply for an air permit. Advocates warn that the move would allow data center developers and other industries to break ground without giving nearby residents a say, or even a warning that construction is planned.
“You can see why that would be so interesting to an administration that wants to rush through the construction of data centers,” says Keri Powell, senior attorney and air program leader at the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC). “What EPA would be allowing would be all of those facilities to go through and just not have to deal with the public, issue the permits in secret behind closed doors. Nobody knows what’s happening until the bulldozers are out there.”
“Nobody knows what’s happening until the bulldozers are out there.”
The EPA’s proposed changes apply to a permitting process that’s been in place since the 1970s called New Source Review that applies to a wide range of facilities, from landfills and paper mills to power plant expansions. More recently with the rise of generative AI, these permits have also become a flashpoint for opposition to new data centers, as well as to power plants built to provide electricity for all those servers.
In July, the EPA announced that it would eliminate the federal public participation requirement for a large set of polluters and place that burden on states. The plan would leave it up to state and local air agencies to decide whether or not to notify the public about certain new sources of pollution — leaving advocates concerned that many of these agencies would forgo the process altogether. Air pollution is often regulated at the federal level because it can waft across the country, affecting residents in one state even if the source is in another.
“The state and local authorities closest to the issues and the public should be making the decisions on the permitting process as much as possible, not Washington,” EPA administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement at the time. “We are cutting unnecessary and burdensome red tape.”
The change applies to so-called “minor” sources of pollution, which the EPA says in its announcement “have relatively low emissions and limited environmental impact.” Powell’s group contends that the “minor” label is a misnomer and that the permitting process routinely covers projects that can have significant consequences for their neighbors.
Colossus 1, xAI’s massive data center in Tennessee that the company billed as the “most powerful AI training system yet,” applied for a minor source permit in 2025. That led to a hearing and elicited thousands of comments to a public notice posted by the local health department, Inside Climate News reported last year. The SELC and NAACP threatened to sue xAI for installing unpermitted gas turbines at the site the same year.
SELC was one of nearly 200 health and environmental groups that filed comments last Friday asking the EPA to withdraw its proposal on New Source Review. They argue that by mandating public comment, residents can provide agencies with valuable insight on the repercussions of building a new data center or other industrial facility.
“[The EPA’s proposal] could deprive the agencies making decisions about these [pollution] sources the necessary lived experience data of those communities. Without that information, it is impossible for permitting agencies to evaluate the full, cumulative impact of these facilities,” Kentucky Resources Council Senior Attorney Byron Gary said in a press release.
The public comment period for the EPA’s proposal ended last week, and EPA spokesperson Carolyn Holran says in an email to The Verge that they’re still reviewing all the comments submitted — more than 4,900 that need to be addressed before the agency can finalize its rule.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction
- Published
Once the undisputed giant of Nigerian politics, the Peoples Democratic Party now finds itself on the brink of extinction.
A question hanging over the campaign for January's general election, which officially kicked off this week, is whether the PDP can survive.
A factional struggle that has ended up in the courts over who exactly is in charge could end up rendering it irrelevant at the ballot box.
It is a remarkable fall for the party, founded in 1998, which appeared impregnable after the end of military rule a year later - so much so that its chairman boasted in 2008 that it would govern for six decades.
For 16 years, it controlled the presidency - in the shape of Olusegun Obasanjo, Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and then Goodluck Jonathan - and the vast majority of the country's 36 states.
But the 2015 federal election was a seismic shock.
The PDP lost the presidential vote to Muhammadu Buhari and the newly formed All Progressives Congress (APC) - a coalition of opposition parties and disgruntled former members.
Thrust into the political wilderness the party's national leaders were bewildered - familiar with the trappings of federal power they had to work out what to do in opposition.
This was the beginning of the end, according to political analyst Ishaq Buhari.
"They were a party that was so used to power, being in opposition was a new challenge they struggled with from the start," he told the BBC.
If 2015 was a major blow, 2025 was the year the party's foundations were left in ruins.
It was marked by a dizzying wave of defections and bitter internal conflicts.
A group of state governors switched party allegiance, which had a particularly devastating effect.
At the start of that year, the PDP still held eight states. But by December, five state governors - from Delta, Akwa Ibom, Enugu, Bayelsa and Rivers - had gone over to the ruling APC.
They cited the PDP's declining viability and a desire for better co-operation with the federal government as reasons for their departure.
Early this year, the PDP held three states but that is now down to zero - with the Oyo governorship slipping from the party's hands just last month.
Internal power struggles, factionalism, insistence that power rotates through the regions and disciplinary measures have all added to the sense of disillusionment within the party.
The PDP has been robbed of high-profile figures and talent, including the loss of former Vice-President Atiku Aubakar last year.
The crisis was intensified by a debilitating leadership tussle.
In November 2025, a faction of the party, which observers say represented the majority of members, held a contentious national convention in Ibadan, Oyo state, despite court orders attempting to stop it.
The convention expelled Nyesom Wike, a prominent PDP member who is serving in President Bola Tinubu's APC-led government.
Wike, who helped found the party, heads a rival faction creating a political stand-off that has paralysed the PDP.
He had controversially helped the APC win Rivers state in the last presidential election leading to accusations that he had betrayed the PDP.
But in the eyes of the law the faction that he heads is the legitimate party.
This means that it has been able to submit its slate of presidential and parliamentary candidates to the electoral commission leaving the rival faction without any representatives on the ballot.
Despite the chaos, some die-hard loyalists remain optimistic.
Politician and staunch PDP member Aminu Adamu, part of the anti-Wike faction, believes a return to its former glory is possible.
He cites examples from Thailand and Argentina, where parties have bounced back after years in the wilderness.
"We have seen it happen before," he tells the BBC. "All we need to do is put our house in order and start to build from there.
"If we make all the necessary corrections, by 2032 I really think PDP can be a major force again."
Others point out that the party still has a grassroots network - essential to win and sustain power - with offices, activists, supporters and local leaders. But by 2032 it may be too late.
With the party in such disarray and candidates backed by Wike on the ballot - voters are unlikely to trust them.
Analyst Deji Olarenwaju believes the only thing that could save the once-mighty party is an alliance with the African Democratic Congress - now seen as the biggest opposition group or Peter Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
"Because on their own they are going nowhere," he says.
