Zhao, a 30-something woman living in Beijing, says she lost over $100,000 in May to a romance scammer who claimed to be a researcher working for Microsoft. After initially chatting Zhao up on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu, he asked to move their conversation to Microsoft Teams, where he was happy to provide her with an account and password she could use.
“I didn’t think much because I had used this app before. And since it was developed by Microsoft, I kind of trusted it,” says Zhao, who requested to use only her last name for privacy reasons.
Once they switched to Teams, the scammer began promising to build a future with Zhao when they eventually got together and introduced her to a cryptocurrency investment project, which he said would turn a profit much faster than trading stocks. Zhao says that at first, she was excited about the opportunity, and even took out loans from several banks so she could invest more.
Then the scammer disappeared with all of her money. Because she can no longer log into the Teams account he told her to use, she can’t share the chat logs with police.
After Zhao began talking about her experience on social media, she says she started hearing from dozens of other people in China who have fallen prey to the same scheme. They claim to have lost anywhere from $1,500 to $300,000, and only one reported that they were able to recover some of the funds—by tracking down the recipient’s bank account.
The victims all describe the same pattern. At some point, they were instructed to download Microsoft Teams and log in using credentials provided by the scammers. The tactic has become so common that some local law enforcement bureaus in China have issued warnings explicitly naming Teams as a tool used by scammers, with one even describing it as a “fraud-related app.” Maimai, a Chinese platform similar to LinkedIn, told Chinese media outlets last year that if it detected high-risk keywords in messages like “Teams” and “Skype,” it would automatically warn users about how to avoid getting scammed.
For years, alleged scam victims have been writing angry reviews of Microsoft Teams on Chinese app stores, some warning others not to download it. WIRED analyzed the past 18 months of reviews of Teams on Apple’s Chinese app store, and found that out of 500, 30 percent included explicit complaints about scammers. The oldest review calling out scams dated all the way back to 2022.
“The scammers had me register for this app so they could contact me, and they defrauded me of RMB 1.48 million [$220,000]. The police have opened a case,” reads one review from January of this year. “This was unquestionably a ‘pig-butchering’ scam. Beware of fraud—this was a bitter and costly lesson!”
Microsoft says scammers routinely exploit trusted brands and communication platforms to carry out social engineering schemes. As these tactics evolve, the company says it “investigates reports of abuse, takes action against accounts that violate our policies, and continues to strengthen protections designed to identify and disrupt fraudulent activity,” Steven Masada, the global head of Microsoft’s digital crimes division, said in a statement to WIRED.
In June, Microsoft started displaying a general warning banner to Teams users in China cautioning them about common scams and urging them to be careful when sharing sensitive information. The company also discontinued the personal version of Teams in China, and the service is now only available in the country through enterprise accounts.
On Chinese social media, people have also reported experiencing variations of the scam involving other corporate software apps, including Webex, a video conferencing platform owned by Cisco, and Cliq, a workplace communication app owned by the Indian software giant Zoho. Since February 2025, 71 percent of the over 150 reviews of Webex on Apple’s Chinese app store referenced being scammed on the platform, according to WIRED’s analysis. Cisco did not respond to a request for comment.
Sam Wunderl, a spokesperson for Zoho, says the company has identified “a limited number of instances involving scammers using Zoho Cliq to defraud victims.” The company says it uncovered the suspicious usage internally. As of August 27, Zoho says it disabled online payments to Cliq in China, suspended every account created by the suspected scammer it identified, and plans to discontinue the free version of Cliq in China going forward.
All Roads Go to Teams
According to dozens of victim accounts shared on Chinese social media platforms like Xiaohongshu and Douyin, the scammers look for new targets seemingly anywhere they can. They pose as job recruiters looking to fill open positions, prospective renters contacting landlords, potential dates on Tinder, and international buyers looking to source products from Chinese factories.
The scammers take advantage of Teams’ enterprise features by creating accounts for their targets and sending them pre-made login credentials. Because the scammers control the organization, they can deactivate the accounts once the scheme is over, wiping out victims’ access to chat histories that could be potentially used as evidence. To explain the unusual setup, scammers may tell victims they’re using work devices that only allow certain apps, or say they created a private Teams account just for the two of them to chat.
It turned out that some of the other victims who contacted Zhao had encountered the very same scammer she had. One was able to share Teams login credentials with her. This time, Zhao pretended to be a new potential victim in order to hopefully trick the scammer into providing more information about how his ruse worked.
She asked why he had to use Teams instead of WeChat, by far the most popular messaging app in China. The scammer claimed his colleagues could see his WeChat messages because he was on a work project, so Teams “is like our secret base together.” The account he gave Zhao, he said, was “for team members to contact family while on the project.”
“Can I ask a small question. What’s the special meaning about my account ‘joy20706905?’” Zhao asked, referring to the username he provided. “The account was assigned by the software when you purchase it from Microsoft,” he responded.
Zhao says when she was defrauded in May, Microsoft Teams didn’t alert her that the conversation she was having with the scammer might be dangerous. It was only when she talked to him again in August that the app started showing a banner that reads: “Don’t share confidential info or your screen with people you don’t know. Report anything suspicious.”
Why Teams?
In many ways, Microsoft Teams is an ideal app for fraudsters in China. Unlike Telegram or WhatsApp, it isn’t blocked by the government. And it has advanced tools like screen sharing and remote control that allow scammers to potentially gain more control over their victims’ devices. Most importantly, it’s a legitimate workplace communication app made by a trusted multinational tech company.
The same factors also apply to Webex. Tan Chenxin, a Chinese software engineer living in New York, says he was nearly defrauded earlier this week after he received a call from someone claiming to be working on a joint police investigation with US Customs and Border Protection and Chinese law enforcement. They asked Tan to download Webex and hop on a video call to discuss the situation. “I looked up Webex and found that it was developed by Cisco, a world-leading cybersecurity software provider,” Tan says. “I happen to know what Cisco is, so I convinced myself it was fine.”
Luckily, he realized it was a scam and hung up before transferring any money. Tan says he couldn’t find a way to easily report the scammer’s account to Webex.
Compared to Chinese messaging apps, which have had to deal with rampant investment fraud scams for years, Western platforms appear less prepared to combat the issue. Apps like WeChat and Xiaohongshu, for example, frequently flag scam risks to users when they detect keywords related to investments and payments, including in private conversations. Even WIRED’s chats with scam victims on Xiaohongshu triggered repeated warnings as they recounted how they had been defrauded.

Today, we look at how a China biotech crackdown could benefit Europe, what a rival drug failure might mean for Alnylam, the algorithm behind the Moderna-Merck cancer vaccine, and a landmark approval in pancreatic cancer.
RIP, Tim Curry. I shall mourn how humbly you buttle.
The need-to-know this morning
- Moderna is raising $2 billion in convertible debt. The new financing comes one week after the Phase 3 success of its personalized cancer vaccine.
The power of the Moderna-Merck cancer vaccine may hinge on an algorithm
Moderna and Merck’s personalized cancer vaccine could become the first approved medicine whose genetic instructions are essentially written by an algorithm. For each patient, software analyzes thousands of tumor mutations and chooses 34 neoantigens to encode into a bespoke mRNA vaccine — a regulatory and computational experiment that some researchers now believe could be the treatment’s “secret sauce.”
That said, some skeptical Wall Street investors think that perhaps the personalization isn’t necessary at all, and that mRNA itself primes tumors to respond better to Keytruda. So what’s in that algorithm?
“I have no idea,” said Alex Rubinsteyn, a cancer vaccine expert at the University of North Carolina. “Everyone claims what they have is proprietary intelligence.”
U.S. crackdown on Chinese biotech could benefit Europe
A bipartisan bill aimed at limiting U.S. biotech ties with China could end up handing Europe a competitive advantage, executives from the Croatia-based CRO Optimapharm opine for STAT. The proposed Biotech Investment National Security Act, or BINSA, would broaden federal oversight of U.S. investment and dealmaking with Chinese biotech companies. However, Optimapharm’s argue, companies could simply route the drugs discovered in China through European sponsors — a strategy dubbed “Eurowashing.”
This potentially could shift licensing profits, tax revenue, and clinical development activity away from the U.S. Also, biotechs often default to crowded U.S., Australian, and Western European trial sites rather than considering faster and cheaper alternatives in Central and Eastern Europe. Whether BINSA passes or not, the executives say, companies should diversify their clinical trial strategies now before geopolitical tensions make those decisions for them.
A heart drug failure casts shadow over Alnylam
The European Society of Cardiology Congress in Munich could offer crucial clues about the future of Alnylam’s ATTR-CM franchise, STAT’s Adam Feuerstein writes. AstraZeneca and Ionis will reveal details on why their rival gene-silencing drug, eplontersen, failed a pivotal Phase 3 study.
The drug showed no cardiovascular benefit when added to widely used stabilizer drugs — which suggests that injectable gene silencers may not add much benefit to much to easier-to-use oral treatments.
This will matter for Alnylam’s blockbuster, Amvuttra, and especially next-generation nucresiran, now in Phase 3 testing. Alnylam says nucresiran’s greater potency and differently designed trial can succeed where eplontersen stumbled, but investors aren’t entirely convinced.
FDA approves landmark pancreatic cancer drug
The FDA has approved the buzzy pancreatic cancer drug made by Revolution Medicines. Rasonque is the first treatment to attack a genetic driver of pancreatic cancer — and what oncologists are calling the disease’s biggest therapeutic advance in decades.
In a pivotal trial, the RAS-targeting drug nearly doubled median survival to 13.2 months from 6.7 months with chemotherapy in previously treated patients. This establishes a new standard of care for a cancer with a dismal 8% five-year survival rate. The approval also caps a decades-long effort to drug the once-considered “undruggable” RAS proteins and transforms Revolution into a leader in targeted cancer medicines.
The drug will cost $39,800 per month and carries substantial skin and mouth toxicities, and patients eventually develop resistance. But it could potentially have benefits in other RAS-driven tumors, including lung and colorectal cancers.

New Delhi, Aug 28: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday greeted people on Raksha Bandhan and hoped that the auspicious festival brings happiness, prosperity and success to everyone's lives.
Raksha Bandhan is a Hindu festival that celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters. On the occasion, sisters tie vibrant threads, or rakhis, on their brothers' wrists as a symbol of their heartfelt prayers and well wishes, and brothers reciprocate with thoughtful gifts and promise to protect them under all circumstances.
"Happy Raksha Bandhan. May this auspicious festival bring happiness, prosperity, and success to all your lives," Modi said in an X post in Hindi.
The prime minister also wished that the bond of affection, togetherness and mutual trust remains eternal.

When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.
The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.
For families who say they lost their children to education system mismanagement and examination scandals, watching the protest scenes unfold on television came with mixed feelings. Some were happy that future students may be spared the same fate; others questioned why it had taken so long.
The Guardian spoke to four families about what happened to their children and how they feel today.
Anshika Pandey, 20, Delhi
Anshika Pandey, the eldest of twin sisters and four siblings, was, her father says, the calmest, quietest and most responsible member of the family. Revision books still lie neatly stacked, bags and accreditation cards hang from the nails where they were last placed. Her ambition was to be a doctor in the community where she lived, to be able to help the “poor people in need of medical care” some day.
Pandey studied for more than 12 hours every day, worked part-time at a store for nearly six hours and slept no more than five hours each night.
This year’s national eligibility cum entrance test (Neet) to gain entrance to medical training was her third attempt at becoming a doctor. After sitting the exam on 3 May, she was hopeful. But on 12 May she learned that the exam had been leaked for the second year in a row and there would be a resit.
“Anshika was deeply hurt. She had been hoping to enter college this year and was happy with the exam she had taken. Still, after cancellation, when I tried to console her, all she lamented was how could she hope to give another good exam,” says her father, Indradhar Pandey, a cab driver in Delhi.
Anshika remained calm and performed her household duties and engaged with everyone normally. But two days later, on 14 May, when everyone had left for work and her twin sister and younger brother were napping, she hanged herself.
Anshika’s dream had been to move her family, especially her siblings, from the slum where they lived. Her younger sister, Pragati, hopes to fulfil that dream and reminisces about how the two sisters had talked about it several times.
Anshika’s sketches and positive messages and mantra chants on the walls of their home, which she wrote to motivate herself, are now the memories her family is refusing to let go of.
Sufi Shaheen, 19, Delhi
Before leaving the house on the morning of 25 October 2024, Sufi Shaheen straightened her hair and put on her favourite jeans. As she left, she asked her mother for 10 rupees (8p), unlike other days when she would ask for 100. Then she headed for her joint entrance examination (Jee) lesson.
Her mother, Sultana Khatoon, asked her why she was leaving the house on an empty stomach. Shaheen replied she would be back soon. Twenty minutes later, she jumped from the seventh floor of a tutoring centre, about a mile away from her home.
It has been almost two years since she died, but Khatoon has not recovered from that day. She is being treated for severe depression and bouts of headaches.
“She was my only daughter of the four children and more like a friend. Every time I stepped out of the house, she would help me get ready. Even though she was deeply passionate about studying and becoming an engineer, she also loved dressing up and made everyone in the house do it too,” says Khatoon, as she looks through her daughter’s school photos.
Living with her parents and three brothers on her father’s modest income as a technical engineer, Shaheen had dreamed of becoming a software engineer and “excelling even more than the boys in her community”, says her mother.
A quick learner and highly motivated, Shaheen taught herself to draw and paint, and even learned to speak Japanese and Korean. But she had been stressed for several months and feared not being able to clear her second attempt at the national engineering entrance exam in January 2025.
When India’s National Testing Agency made changes to the Jee exam syllabus, Shaheen couldn’t sleep for days. She remained stressed, cried when talking to her brother and her best friend on the phone, and wrote a note to her parents in which she apologised and asked her younger brother, Masoom, to make their dreams come true.
“Almost two years later, Masoom was ranked 188th in the whole of India in his CUET [common university entrance test]. But we do not have Shaheen to celebrate this with,” says Khatoon.
Pradeep Kumar Mahich, 22, Rajasthan
“Even God will not be able to stop me from becoming a doctor this year,” were 22-year-old Pradeep Mahich’s words to his father right after his Neet exam on 3 May. This was his fourth attempt and, most importantly, he felt confident. But the announcement of the exam paper leak and resit broke his heart.
No one in the family had ever “dreamt so big”, says Pradeep’s father, Rajesh Kumar, a farmer in Rajasthan’s Sikar district. Kumar sold a large part of his farmland and took a loan of 11 lakhs (£8,600) under the farmer’s crop loan schemes.
“Sikar, the main coaching hub for Neet, is only an hour and a half from our village. My eldest daughter, Babita, who was preparing to join the police, and my son were both studying in Sikar, renting an apartment. This was his fourth year of tutoring, and the money from selling the land and the loan was slowly being consumed. I would send monthly expenses of £250 and Pradeep’s annual tutoring fees of £4,000, asking them not to worry about money and focus on his studies,” says Kumar.
“Pradeep had told me, ‘Papa, we will do a big celebration before I go to college. And one day I’ll return to serve the people of the village,’” says Kumar.
On 15 May, as he did every day, Kumar sent milk and curd to his two children on a bus that goes to Sikar; Pradeep came to pick it up at 9.30am then went home and told his sister he would help prepare lunch. But when his sister was showering, he hanged himself. She has taken a break from her studies and returned home.
Seeing students protesting on his television screen, Kumar says he is relieved that the eduction minister has gone but says there should be a proper investigation so that “no family suffers the same fate that we did”.
S Anitha, 17, Tamil Nadu
S Anitha belonged to an underprivileged lower caste, or Dalit, community from Tamil Nadu’s Ariyalur district. Born to a daily wage labourer, her mother died when she was seven, leaving her grandparents to raise her.
As a teenager, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. “At such a tender age, she was so focused that we used to feel proud of her,” says her brother, Manirathinam. “She knew what she wanted and never distracted herself with anything else. She never asked for any clothes, jewellery or food – her focus was clear and she knew the circumstances.”
She scored a perfect 100 in physics and chemistry at school and was offered a place to study aeronautical engineering at the state’s technological institute. But when she could not even meet the cut-off marks in the Neet exam, she realised that she had been studying a different syllabus.
Tamil Nadu had already criticised the national government for imposing an all-India examination – “disrupting the federal structure” – because it had a different education system. As a result, the state was exempted from Neet in 2016, but not in 2017, the year Anitha sat the exam.
When the supreme court ruled on 22 August 2017 that admissions to medical school would be based only on the Neet exam, she lost hope. On 1 September, Anitha hanged herself in her grandparents’ home. Her suicide became the subject of a public debate and led to widespread protests across the state and even in Delhi.
Her brother took part in last month’s protests in the capital and, while happy about the Indian education minister’s resignation in July, argues that all exams should become state-run, rather than by central government, as not everyone can afford the hefty tutoring fees needed to sit the Neet exam.
He now runs a free library and education centre in Anitha’s name.

Apple is making it more expensive for Americans to watch Shrinking, Ted Lasso, Pluribus, and its growing catalogue of original films and shows, with the company raising subscription prices in the US from Friday, 28 August. The monthly Apple TV subscription will now cost $14.99, up from $12.99, while the annual plan has increased to $119 from $99. The new rates apply to both new and existing subscribers. Apple said existing customers will be notified approximately one month before they are charged the new price. This is the fourth price increase for Apple TV, formerly known as Apple TV+, in four years. The latest rise also puts the service at three times its original monthly price of $4.99, which was introduced when Apple launched the platform in 2019 with a much smaller library. There is another increase for customers who use Apple One. The individual tier of the bundle, which includes Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud+ with 50 GB of storage and Apple Arcade, is rising from $19.95 to $21.95 a month. The move comes amid a broader reset in the streaming market. Prices have been climbing across the industry as services attempt to improve profitability and offset the substantial cost of producing and acquiring content. Netflix, HBO Max, Disney+, Hulu, Paramount+ and YouTube Premium have all raised prices over the past two years. NBCUniversal’s Peacock increased its rates earlier this month, while ESPN is due to raise its streaming prices from 17 September. Apple TV remains unusual among the major premium streaming platforms because it does not currently offer an ad-supported subscription tier. The price increases also come as Apple’s streaming operation has expanded considerably since its launch. Apple TV now carries more than 300 original television shows and films, compared with the handful of titles available when the service first debuted. Its catalogue includes comedy series Ted Lasso, The Studio and Shrinking, alongside drama and thriller titles such as Severance, Pluribus and The Morning Show. This year, Widow’s Bay became the most Emmy-nominated freshman series. For Apple, the higher prices mark another step in the evolution of a service that initially relied on a relatively small collection of prestige programming to draw subscribers. The latest increase takes effect immediately for new customers, while existing subscribers will move to the higher rates after receiving advance notice. While mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are more than capable of helping with the basics, dedicated AI interview tools take things a step further. We tested eight such tools that offer everything from resume-based interview questions and technical interview practice to video analysis, peer interviews, and detailed feedback. Here is how they work, which one you should choose, and how to get the most out of them.

How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. Fortunately, this groundwork only requires leveraging existing AI tools you may already be using. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. AI can not only identify potential loopholes but also help you present your projects to the interviewer in the most convincing way possible. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.
Foremost, your prompt should include information about the company’s current market position. You can assist the AI model by attaching the company’s press releases, financial reports, product launch notes, public announcements, and more. Financial reports can also be used to project the company’s future trends, map future goals, and more, which are worth knowing about.
It’s also essential to understand the company’s competitors, as it can help you frame your answers to interview questions in the company’s favor. While you are unlikely to find many, you can ask the AI model to identify and propose viable solutions to the company’s publicly available problems. It can be a significant advantage when handled appropriately and also serves as a good background for obvious questions, such as “What will you bring to the table?” and “Why should we hire you?”
→ Analyze the Interviewer
If you know who will be interviewing you, publicly available professional information can help you prepare better. Their LinkedIn profile, current role, past experience, or area of expertise may give you a fair idea of which parts of your background they are more likely to focus on.
You can provide this information to an AI model and ask it to suggest questions that someone in a similar role may ask. Don’t treat those questions as predictions, though. Use them simply to broaden your preparation and identify areas you may otherwise overlook.
This information is also useful when preparing questions to ask towards the end of the interview. Relevant questions about their team, role, or experience with the company will usually come across better than generic ones.
→ Generate Behavioral, Situational, and Technical Interview Questions
A recommended way to ensure success in an interview is to prepare for the likely questions. The question set should not only include the basic ones, but also challenging ones to put you on the spot. That way, your real-world performance will be sufficient for selection. To begin with, the basics: you can ask AI models to generate common behavioral interview questions, such as “Introduce yourself” and “Why should we hire you?” “What if we don’t select you?” “What makes you fit for this role?” and the like.
The answers to the above questions will be based on your resume and cognitive ability, which is what AI models can help you with. Next, to tackle the technical questions, your prompt must instruct the AI model to fire deep-dive technical, situational, and project-based questions at you. During all this, you can rate your technical skills and promptly improve any weak areas.
Despite the discomfort, ask the AI model to generate questions from the perspective of an interviewer who is not interested in hiring you. Understand the questions, as they can prove to be great at identifying gaps in your resume, incompetencies, and more. You can also ask the AI model to question the relevance of your past experiences, push back aggressively on your answers, and more. This will only improve your chances of getting selected.
→ Practice Mock Interviews With AI Voice Mode
In case you are unaware, most mainstream AI models offer voice modes that are perfect for back-and-forth questioning, making them ideal for interview practice. It’s not surprising that merely reading the questions and thinking you can answer them won’t cut it, which is why you need a simulation of the interview. It may cause you to memorize answers instead of coming up with your own, which may result in you sounding like a teleprompter, or worse, freezing on the spot if you forget the exact answer, leaving a bad impression.
Voice mode is best used on the mobile versions of AI agents. First, you must tell the AI its persona by verbally describing it, uploading the job description, interview details, or any other supporting documents. We also recommend uploading your resume to ensure a curated interaction. Next, you must instruct it to ask all types of questions, including behavioral, technical, and situation-based.
Remember, the purpose of this mock interview is to prepare you for the worst, so take away critical lessons and improve yourself. For this, you can ask the AI model to rate your answers and provide you with detailed assessments to help you identify your weak points. Not only will it cure the interview phobia that you may have, but it will also improve your speaking skills, conversational awareness, and your ability to answer curveballs.

Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.
Excel in Interviews With These AI Tools
AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Exponent Practice and Interviewing.io make more sense for technical candidates, Yoodli is particularly good for communication and behavioral practice, while MyInterviewAI works well for resume-based preparation. Big Interview helps with overall delivery, Huru AI makes quick job-specific practice easy, and Ophy AI covers the widest range of interview-preparation needs.
Whichever tool you choose, don’t stop after one mock interview. Upload your latest resume and the actual job description, complete a practice session, review where you struggled, and repeat it after fixing those areas. Two or three focused mock interviews will be far more useful than memorizing dozens of AI-generated answers.
Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.

The world’s first patient to undergo brain surgery with live artificial intelligence assistance has had his tumour successfully removed, the BBC reported.
Rhys Hibbert, a 48-year-old father of two from Bedfordshire, underwent the pioneering procedure at University College London Hospital. Surgeons said he could have lost his sight as the tumour was pressing on his optic nerves.
The AI system analysed a live video feed during the operation and identified the likely location of crucial blood vessels and nerves, helping surgeons determine the safest areas from which to remove the tumour.
Hibbert had an 11mm non-cancerous tumour on his pituitary gland, which sits close to the carotid arteries and optic nerves. His peripheral vision had begun to narrow, while he also suffered from fatigue and dizziness.
The operation was performed through the nose using an endoscope. The tumour was partly hidden behind bone and a tough membrane, making it difficult for surgeons to identify the safest route for removal.
The experimental AI tool, described as being similar to a “surgical ChatGPT”, tracked surgical instruments and highlighted important anatomical structures on a second screen in real time.
Prof Hani Marcus, one of the surgeons, said the system had been trained using hundreds of videos of pituitary tumour operations and could act as an “expert second pair of eyes”.
However, the surgeons retained full control of the procedure. The research team, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research and Google, now plans a larger clinical trial. Hibbert said his vision had improved significantly after the operation. “It’s given me my life back,” he told the BBC.

GTA 6 is making police pursuits smarter, more persistent, and far more dangerous than anything you have experienced in the previous GTA titles. However, the latest GTA 6 Extended Look on Netflix actually reveals some surprisingly simple ways to evade the police before it turns into a citywide disaster.
The primary thing to know here is what the police in GTA 6 can actually recognize. As revealed by Rockstar, there needs to be witnesses who report a crime, or a certain alarm needs to go off for the cops to go after you.
Once the crime gets reported, officers can identify the suspect’s appearance, clothing, and vehicle with these details represented by icons beneath the wanted level. If the police recognize your vehicle in GTA 6, simply abandoning it and taking another ride can remove one of the biggest clues.
In the GTA 6 preview on Netflix, Lucia does the same by setting up the identified car on fire and taking another van to flee the wanted situation.
Rockstar explains that the same idea applies to your appearance. Simply wearing a mask while committing a crime can prevent the police from receiving a description of your face. Moreover, if you also try changing into a different outfit, it will disrupt the cops’ knowledge of what you were wearing.
Now, if the wanted level goes beyond three stars, things start to get quite serious. It gets increasingly difficult to navigate the busy streets, and it might get you ‘Busted‘ before you know it. If that does happen, you can try leaving behind vehicles and using alleys, side streets, or simply jumping over fences to flee the police and fall off the radar.
Another important aspect is that officers can tell if the two GTA 6 protagonists, Jason and Lucia, are partners in a crime. So, if the two-person icon shows up beneath the wanted star level, make sure to split up to divide the police’s attention.
Lastly, two more icons that can appear beneath the star level: the CCTV and the weapon icon. While the former states that a nearby camera has captured your face, the latter states that you’re an armed criminal.
In order to get away from such situations, you can wear the mask before committing the crime so the camera doesn’t capture your face.
One of the biggest changes is that GTA 6 brings back the six-star wanted level, and reaching this level will surely create massive havoc in the city.

How long is a new Fire TV Stick actually supposed to last?
A Fire TV Stick can outlive its guaranteed support window, though aging apps and hardware may make you want to replace it sooner.
There isn't an expiration date hidden in the settings menu of a Fire TV Stick. Amazon also doesn't reveal a typical physical lifespan for its streaming sticks, nor does it inform owners to replace one after three, four or five years. That makes the question of "how long will it last?" a bit more complicated than it sounds.
At least one of the numbers is firm. Amazon says security updates are provided for at least four years from the date the Fire TV device was purchased new from Amazon as the seller, or until the support date listed for that model, whichever is later. The Fire TV Stick 4K Select and Fire TV Stick 4K Plus are among the current models with security updates guaranteed through at least Dec. 31, 2030.
Amazon doesn't call it a lifespan, though. A support deadline indicates the duration of security fixes, not when the hardware will decide it has streamed its last episode.
Four years is a minimum, but it's not a countdown to the junk drawer.
Four years isn't an expiration date
The Fire TV Stick can be fully functional beyond the security-update window, but simply turning on isn't a very high standard for a streaming device. Older hardware can become increasingly uncomfortable to use as apps become more demanding, interfaces evolve and video standards advance, even if nothing has failed internally.
Video codecs are a part of that. Newer video codecs like H.265/HEVC and AV1 can compress video more efficiently than older codecs, but they also need the right decoding hardware. The Plus doesn't have an advantage on that front, as Amazon's current Fire TV Stick 4K Select and 4K Plus both offer hardware decoding for AV1 and H.265 at up to 4K60.
Apps can be less accommodating. Netflix itself notes that its app may no longer be available on some TVs and streaming devices made before 2015, providing a neat example of what aging really looks like for a streamer: The hardware can still work, while one of the reasons you bought it quietly stops working with it.
That doesn't mean every Fire TV Stick has a 10-year lifespan, but it does show why declaring one "dead" simply because four years have passed is difficult to justify.
When should you actually replace your Fire TV Stick?
Slower streaming performance isn't necessarily a retirement notice, either. Before giving up on your Fire TV Stick, Amazon suggests restarting it, installing available updates, clearing app caches and ruling out network issues. Insufficient power can also cause restarts, making a healthy stick look much more dramatic than it is.
Persistent problems are more convincing. Apps crashing repeatedly, services dropping support for your model, menus staying slow after troubleshooting or storage becoming a constant hassle are signs that an upgrade may actually help.
Buying slightly higher up the range can give you more breathing room. The Fire TV Stick 4K Select has 1GB of RAM and costs about $40, while the 4K Plus has 2GB for about $50. Amazon warns that memory pressure can kill apps on lower-memory Fire TV hardware, so that extra $10 buys more headroom as software gets heavier.
It doesn't guarantee an extra year or two, and Amazon makes no such claim. The Select's Vega OS has an efficient footprint and was designed to scale across devices. Still, doubling the RAM for roughly the price of lunch is worth considering if you'll keep the stick for years.
And then there's the remote. Its two AAA batteries will need replacing, and a failed remote can be replaced separately. Amazon's Fire TV mobile app can control the streamer too, so a dead remote doesn't necessarily mean a dead Fire TV Stick.
Netflix discontinued support for first-generation Fire TV and Fire TV Stick devices in June 2025, The Verge reported, more than 10 years after they launched in 2014.

Protests against reservations were held at Jantar Mantar and Connaught Place in Delhi on 21 and 23 August 2026. The protests were part of an online campaign called the ‘Reservation Hatao Andolan’, which has over 5.6 million followers on Instagram. The protestors primarily demanded that government jobs and opportunities in educational institutions be provided based on financial status and merit, rather than caste. They also demanded the withdrawal of the 2026 Equity Regulations, which were brought in by the UGC to control discrimination in higher educational institutions.
In this context, a video of a huge crowd blocking a road is being shared on social media, claiming to show the protest at Jantar Mantar on 21 August 2026, demanding the withdrawal of the UGC Equity Regulations, 2026. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of massive crowd at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, protesting against reservations and demanding a rollback of the UGC Equity Regulations on 21 August 2026.
Fact: The video actually depicts a July 2026 farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, demanding minimum support price (MSP) for their Moong crop. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to an identical clip (archive), which was uploaded on the Facebook page of Ramakant Dwivedi on 29 July 2026. The description states that it shows a farmers’ protest in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. We found several other videos of this protest on social media, which can be seen here and here.
The protest site can also be identified on Google Maps as Narmadapuram Road in Bhopal. According to reports (here, here & here), the farmers were protesting to demand 100% procurement of their Moong (green gram) crop at the Minimum Support Price (MSP), among other issues. The farmers marched from Narmadapuram to Bhopal, demanding the abolition of the e-token system for procurement and fertiliser distribution. However, the protest ended after talks with the government.
To sum it up, the viral video depicts a July 2026 farmers’ protest in Bhopal and is falsely being shared as UGC roll back protests in Delhi.

NHRC member Priyank Kanoongo warns schools against restricting mehndi, rakhis
NHRC member Priyank Kanoongo has asked schools not to stop Hindu children from applying mehndi or tying rakhis during Raksha Bandhan. He said these practices are part of religious freedom and warned of action if complaints are received.
Priyank Kanoongo, Member of the National Human Rights Commission, has urged schools not to prevent Hindu children from applying mehndi or tying rakhis during Raksha Bandhan, saying such practices are part of Hindu tradition and religious freedom.
In a post on X, Kanoongo said mehndi washes off within two to four days and rakhis can also be removed, adding that neither practice disrupts school discipline or affects the dress code.
He urged school administrators and managements not to obstruct what he described as the religious freedom rights of Hindu children because of their religious or faith-based choices, warning that action could be taken in case of complaints.
In a Hindi video accompanying the post, Kanoongo shared a photograph of his daughter with mehndi on her hands and said applying mehndi, wearing bangles and tying rakhis during the monsoon festive season are Hindu traditions.
He said children should be allowed to learn and follow these traditions, adding that some schools object to students wearing rakhis or applying mehndi due to religious reasons.
Calling it a basic right of children, Kanoongo said applying mehndi for a few days or tying a rakhi does not harm a school's discipline or traditions. He appealed to schools not to trouble children and warned of strict action if complaints were received.
He also invited parents facing such issues to submit complaints through his official contact.

For crores of Indian families, the financial shock of hospitalisation — especially in a private hospital — begins even before treatment is complete. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare, in its 176th Report tabled in Parliament on August 7, 2026, noted that the average cost of hospitalisation is ₹50,508 in a private facility, compared with ₹6,631 in a government facility. For childbirth, the average out-of-pocket medical expenditure in private facilities is ₹37,630, against ₹2,299 in public facilities.
Some of the contradictions
The committee has made 368 recommendations, including standardised package rates and mandatory pre-treatment cost estimates. Among the widely reported proposals is that basic room tariffs in metropolitan private hospitals should not exceed the average tariff of three-star hotels that are nearby. It has also suggested that large corporate hospitals earning from medical tourism, foreign patients and high-net-worth individuals should cross-subsidise poorer Indians and reserve beds for Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) beneficiaries at regulated rates. Yet, there is a contradiction. India wants more private and foreign capital in health care, particularly in Tier-2, Tier-3 and rural areas, while simultaneously asking the government to review foreign direct investment rules related to the acquisition and management of existing hospitals.
There is a strong case for continued investment in Indian health care. Hospitals require substantial capital. Land, equipment, intensive care units, digital systems, laboratories and trained personnel are expensive. Public hospitals cannot currently meet all demand for secondary and tertiary care. Private hospitals therefore fill an important gap. Foreign investors and private-equity funds can bring capital, managerial capacity, technology and the capacity to expand hospital networks. India also needs investment in pharmaceutical and medical-device manufacturing. If regulation becomes excessively restrictive or unpredictable, some investment may move elsewhere. This could slow capacity expansion and delay the development of better health-care infrastructure in cities and districts where need is genuine.
However, in all sectors, capital comes with expectations of returns. In health care, it creates a special concern because patients are not ordinary consumers. A patient rarely decides independently whether an MRI is required, whether hospital admission should continue for two more days, or whether a procedure is necessary. Health care is shaped by what economists call information asymmetry: the provider knows more than the patient. Therefore, when financial incentives become too strong, they can influence not just the price of care but also how much care is delivered.
A closer look at private care
This is where the role of private equity and venture capital in health care deserves closer attention. Corporate hospital groups increasingly compete for well-known specialists, sophisticated technology and premium infrastructure. These can improve quality, but also create a high-cost ecosystem. Hospitals that pay very high salaries to senior specialists and super-specialists, acquire expensive equipment and operate under pressure to increase revenue must eventually recover these costs. Revenue targets, procedure-linked incentives, higher occupancy expectations and higher revenue per bed can gradually influence institutional behaviour. Most doctors act in patients’ interests. Yet, systems shape behaviour. If hospitals and doctors are rewarded for doing more, the direction becomes predictable.
The result is not only higher cost but also a worrying medicalisation. Lab investigations may detect abnormalities that would never have caused harm. More screening can lead to unnecessary follow-up tests. A patient who could be managed as an outpatient may be admitted. Caesarean sections, angioplasties, intensive-care admissions, diagnostic packages and long lists of medicines must therefore be seen not only as individual clinical decisions but also within the incentive structure of the health system. This does not mean these interventions are usually unnecessary. It means that a system rewarding interventions and procedures needs strong safeguards against unnecessary prescriptions, surgeries, investigations and medications.
That is why a review of FDI in the acquisition of existing hospitals is justified. Domestic investors can be equally profit-oriented, while foreign investment can create valuable capacity. The more useful question is about what an investment does to the health system. Does it create new beds or simply acquire existing ones? Does it improve competition or lead to market concentration? Does it enter an underserved district or add another high-end facility in a metro? If an investor receives concessional land, tax benefits or other public support, are there enforceable obligations related to affordable beds or participation in public insurance schemes? India should encourage greenfield investment and manufacturing, while scrutinising acquisitions that reduce competition or raise the risk of excessive pricing.
Price regulation also needs to be approached carefully. The proposal to link hospital room charges to nearby three-star hotels is easy to understand, but cannot by itself solve the affordability problem. A hospital room includes nursing, infection-control and emergency support that a hotel room does not. More importantly, if one component of the bill is capped, hospitals may increase charges elsewhere. India’s experience with coronary stent price regulation showed that government intervention can reduce excessive mark-ups. But hospital care is more complex; what matters is the total cost of an episode. Package rates, transparent estimates, billing standards and audit mechanisms are therefore more useful than isolated caps on individual components. There is also an established approach to such payments: Diagnosis-Related Groups (DRG). A DRG is a patient-classification system that standardised hospital reimbursement by paying a fixed, predetermined amount for an inpatient stay based on the diagnosis and procedures, rather than reimbursing each service separately.
Focus on public health
There is a larger policy question. India cannot regulate its way out of weak public health care. If government hospitals remain overcrowded, understaffed or difficult to access, citizens will continue to depend heavily on private providers. Experience from OECD countries has shown that one effective form of regulation is a strong public health system that provides a credible alternative.
Public hospitals must therefore become a genuine option, not merely the last resort for those who cannot afford private care. Primary health care needs strengthening so that disease is prevented, detected and treated early. Insurance systems, including AB-PMJAY, should reward appropriate care rather than simply higher volumes of procedures. Clinical audits, evidence-based treatment protocols and transparent billing can protect both patients and doctors from commercial pressures.
The Parliamentary Committee is right to focus attention on affordability and to question whether the current pattern of investment in private health care aligns with public interest. Price caps and an FDI review are reasonable starting points, but India needs a wider conversation about the kind of health-care system it is building. Private investment will remain essential, and profit by itself is not the problem.
The problem begins when the pursuit of returns starts a key influence. A health-care system should attract capital, but its clinical priorities must still be set by medical need. The true measure of India’s health-care progress will not be how much money flows into hospitals or what is the annual compounded growth rate in medical tourism, but whether Indian citizens can enter them with confidence that they will receive what they need. No more, no less.
Chandrakant Lahariya is a practising physician specialising in preventive and cardio-metabolic medicine, whose upcoming book, Pill-Free: You Don’t Need Everything You Have Been Prescribed, will be released in September 2026

Mumbai, August 28, 2026: Observing that young offenders should be given an opportunity to reform and rehabilitate themselves, the Bombay High Court has quashed a 2015 FIR against a man who had allegedly brandished a sword during a confrontation with a mob when he was 19 years old.
Justice Milind Jadhav, while allowing the man’s plea, said punishment should aim at a “reformative result rather than being punitive in nature”. The court noted that the accused was a Class XII student at the time of the incident and had no criminal antecedents.
Incident At Wadala Chawl
The incident took place on June 6, 2014, at a chawl in Wadala following a quarrel between two families. According to the court, around 15-20 members of the Kharat family, along with the complainant, went to the premises looking for members of the Waghmare family. As they were not present, the group entered the room of their relatives, the Kamble family, where the applicant and two women were present.
Neighbouring witnesses told the police that the applicant, who was confronted by the mob, brandished a sword to ward them off. The sword was an award he had received and was displayed in his house. No one was injured in the incident.
Court Considers Reformative Approach
The court said that while the act of holding the sword could, at first glance, appear to amount to criminal intimidation, the circumstances leading to it also had to be considered.
The judge noted that the man had since grown up, was educated and had received an offer of employment from an international shipping company.
“If the applicant is made to languish in jail or face the trial further, there is every possibility that he might lose faith in the institution and society at large and may tread the path of criminality or would waste his life,” Justice Jadhav observed.
The court said every opportunity for a “reformative approach” should be considered in cases involving young offenders so that they get an opportunity to become good citizens and earn their livelihood honourably.

It accordingly quashed the FIR registered at Dadar police station and all consequential proceedings. The police were also directed to consider the court’s order for issuing a police clearance certificate for his employment, provided he had no other offence.
However, the court cautioned against taking the law into one’s hands and imposed a cost of Rs 10,000 on the applicant, to be paid by his father to the Bar Council of Maharashtra and Goa Advocate Aid Fund.

This past week, the top health story, without any doubt, is the huge crisis that is brewing out of proportions in Africa - the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. It was first announced as an outbreak on May 15, this year.As per latest data, it has reached over 5,000 cases, making this the one of the worst Ebola outbreaks in history. The outbreak has clearly outpaced response efforts.
Data from Congo’s Ministry of Health showed the outbreak had so far recorded 5,021 cases, including 2,378 deaths as of August 16, 2026, as it rages in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable fuelled by insecurity, displacement and intense population movements. It has officially infected and killed more people at a greater speed than any other outbreak in history. Starting from the first detected case, it has spread about three times faster than an outbreak from 2014 to 2016 across West Africa, which was the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record with more than 11,000 deaths.
The dire situation was underlined as World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus announced: “We must be frank: the epidemic is far from being under control.” Safety concerns have limited the response as health workers are targeted, particularly in Ituri, the province that has been hit the worst by the outbreak. Residents recently attacked a health team in the territory of Aru after a suspected case was reported there. A mob set fire to an ambulance and damaged two other vehicles, according to Michael Wani, president of the Union of Cultural Associations for the Development of Ituri.
Meanwhile, more than 16,000 doses of the new Ebola vaccine Ervebo arrived in the DRC. WHO experts still do not know whether Ervebo protects humans against the Bundibugyo strain, but early data, notably from animal trials, suggest it could offer some protection.The Ervebo vaccine “has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak”, Samuel Roger Kamba, the DRC’s Minister of Health, told the press.
The other big story in India was also about an infectious disease - H1N1. As the cases continue to surge, experts assure that there is no cause for alarm yet. However they do advise that a large number of children were being affected, and that children with asthma and other chronic conditions might require special intervention.
The H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A, and can cause respiratory illness, with symptoms including fever or chills, cough, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, tiredness, and muscle or body aches. In some cases, patients may also experience vomiting and diarrhoea. Cases have been rising in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Kerala, and while there are a number of respiratory-like illnesses also about during this season, doctors have warned that early testing is key. Bindu Shajan Perappadan reports that union Health Minister J.P. Nadda reviewed the H1N1 situation, healthcare preparedness in Delhi.
With National Eye Donation Fortnight being observed across India every year from August 25 to September 8 to raise awareness about eye donation we did our bit to highlight issues relating to eye health a little ahead of schedule.
Athira Elssa Johnson writes about the Lazy eye in children, and about squints. In the former, she focuses on how many parents may miss lazy eye among their children. Often called lazy eye, amblyopia may have no obvious signs and can remain undetected during early childhood. Screening, timely treatment and sustained follow-up are important because visual development is time-sensitive. Squints are another condition that impact the development of vision, and therefore need to be addressed on time. Squint, medically known as strabismus, is a condition in which the two eyes do not align properly. It can affect children and adults and, when it develops during childhood, can interfere with the normal development of vision
In the modern age, the field of ophthalmology is among the earliest adopters of AI systems in health care, so here is an article on using AI systems in smartphones to help detect eye diseases. Kathleen Sherwin and Rishi Raj Borah make an impassioned case for more women to lead eye health care systems.
This week we looked at some little explored aspects of cancer care too. Shrabana Chatterjee writes an interesting story on a hardly-spoken about aspect- Navigating the challenges of fertility and breastfeeding after surviving cancer. This story has a positive message for women in this position - that with careful management and supervision, it can be done.
After a cancer diagnosis, women who have not yet started their families, must be given the option for fertility preservation, say doctors. Options such as embryo freezing before cancer treatment is begun may be considered under medical guidance. Other fertility preservations techniques including oocyte and ovarian-tissue cryopreservation may also be explored before treatment begins. When it comes to breastfeeding, doctors say that after surviving cancer it may pose difficulties, but it can be done under the right medical conditions and with guidance from doctors.
Dr. Siddharth Turkar turns the spotlight on sarcomas: Many soft-tissue sarcomas, which are rare types of cancers that form in fat, muscles and blood vessels, initially look like ordinary lumps. However, when a suspicious mass of this sort is removed without appropriate imaging, tissue diagnosis or oncological planning, the opportunity for the simplest and best-planned first operation may already have been lost.
This is by far the most important gene-based analysis that pertains to us, in India. Rupsy Khurana writes the truth: South Asians are missing from global health databases, and why this matters and what needs to change in this scenario. When scientists try to understand why diseases such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease affect South Asians differently, they often have to rely on genetic data drawn from European populations. Advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning are allowing scientists to mine vast amounts of genomic and health data to detect disease earlier, predict risk, monitor patients and tailor treatments to individuals. But at the heart of this changing landscape lies an old, constant problem – the data used to build these tools lack diversity, she points out.
Further, looking the genetic pool, I write about new research that establishes that natural sugar along with meat consumption powered brain development in early humans. It probably explains the human craving for sweets, today. Read Sugar power: the full story of brain development in humans for more.

It’s safe to say Grand Theft Auto VI is the most anticipated game ever. Thirteen years after the last entry in the series, rampant fervor and speculation about what features the game will include have ratcheted up. Today, Rockstar Games divulged more details through an exclusive livestream event on Netflix called Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look. The spectacle was a 26-minute-long collection of gameplay, cutscenes, and game mechanics.
And boy, does this sure look like a GTA game. The trailer featured Lucia and Jason, the two main characters, driving around Vice City, GTA’s fictional version of Miami. It highlighted all kinds of violence and shenanigans your characters can engage in, and it looks good doing it.
The livestream follows a week of gameplay leaks and story spoilers by the hacker group Cyberleek, which Rockstar called “heartbreaking.” A bevy of other details about the game emerged just a day before the event in a story published by the British magazine Dazed. The piece chronicles the extraordinary level of detail and effort Rockstar has put into GTA VI, including how players control the characters and the unprecedented realism that Rockstar put into its satirical sandbox version of Miami.
It’s bound to be a massive game; today’s reveal shows just how much of a monster it will be. Here are the big takeaways from the livestream.
It Sure Is Pretty
GTA VI is gorgeous. The cityscapes, nightclubs, and lush natural parks shown all seem vibrant and awash in color.
There is a noticeable difference between cutscenes and gameplay, though, as the gameplay clips looked a little flatter and more desaturated than the cinematic cutscenes. That’s kind of a nitpick, though it’s worth noting that in the very first scene—in the dark basement of a crack house—the lighting is so dim it washes out the features of several Black characters around the table.
You Play as 2 Characters Simultaneously
The player can control two characters, Jason and Lucia, a Bonnie-and-Clyde-esque couple who seem to be working out some lingering tension in their relationship as they go about their various criminal activities.
The voice acting for the main characters and other non-playable characters (NPCs) feels tightly written, though that’s based on the select clips Rockstar showed. According to Dazed, the relationship between the characters can change over time, and the player’s actions can affect how that plays out. Keep that in mind if you’re hoping for a particular ending.
GTA VI offers a plethora of options for changing the two main characters’ appearances. Eating too much or too little food affects their weight. Working out can make them swole. The Extended Look also showed off characters eating and working out in minigames. It was a feature in 2004’s GTA San Andreas and in a smaller way in GTA V. Now, that reactivity will be much more fully realized in GTA VI.
There’s also an array of clothes you can equip your characters with, which Rockstar has apparently coordinated with real-life fashion designers to put in the game. Some of these, however, may only come with the $100 Ultimate Edition that people are very mad about.
Maybe Don’t Hit and Run
The NPCs in the game appear much more responsive and interactive than in prior games. According to Dazed, Rockstar has an entire studio in Los Angeles dedicated to working on NPC pedestrian behavior alone.
In the Extended Look, gameplay segments with car chases pointedly avoided streamrolling over pedestrians. But NPCs wore yoga outfits, rode scooters, and seemed to have more personality than the cut-and-paste crowds of past games.
Driving seems greatly improved. When driving, you have a minimap that looks like an actual GPS map guiding you where to go. A car chase saw the main characters running from the police. The player can switch between Lucia and Jason and choose to either drive or shoot at the pursuers. Shooting out tires can cause a car to flip, crash into the sidewalk, and cause environmental destruction.
At one point, a character also body-slams a cop through a wall, which hints at potentially more destructive environments indoors as well. GTA games have been iffy about destructible environments before, though. Sometimes in GTA V you can easily crash through a large light pole but then get instantly stopped by a volleyball net. So we’ll see how reactive everything gets.
So Much Room for Activities
Vice City and the surrounding areas seem absolutely massive. It’s also fully Florida, allowing your characters to fanboat around the Everglades, kayak on the rivers, or scuba dive and jet ski in the Gulf.
One scene from the trailer shows Lucia accidentally kidnapping a livestreaming influencer, then carrying him along through a car chase from the police. Many of the characters use phones and communicate via text. It’s clear that GTA VI has some satirical takes on social media, but we’ll see how relevant it feels in a constantly shifting era.
You Can Pet the Dog
A dog is in at least one scene of the game. Can you pet it? Yes. Yes, you can.
User-Generated Content
In 2023, Rockstar bought the modding marketplace Cfx and reworked it into an official place to share and purchase user-created mods for the game. That service, along with GTA Online’s Rockstar Mission Creator, which lets users make custom levels and modes, indicates that Rockstar has long realized that GTA is fertile ground for user creativity.
The Extended Look didn’t show anything suggesting it would advance those user-creation capabilities, but that’s likely because the game is being released as a single-player title before any multiplayer elements are added.
