The effect of political and religious indoctrination on young minds resembles a slow-release poison. Unfolding in observational vignettes, Pankaj Johar and Sunaina Kapoor’s thought-provoking documentary centres on Vidya Mutth, a prestigious Hindu school in the holy city of Varanasi, India, where sectarian beliefs are drilled into its students, all in the name of cultural preservation.
The film opens with controversial speeches made by the school’s spiritual leader, Guru Avimuktesh, who advocates the abolition of religious freedom, and for Indian Muslims to either convert to Hinduism or leave for Pakistan. A prominent Hindu figure with a large following, he personally oversees the entrance exam, a sequence captured in dynamic handheld shots. While boys take the test, their parents look on with apprehension and anxiety; to be accepted would be an honour, not only for their child but for the whole family.
For those who do get in to Vidya Mutth, what follows is far from a glorious, enlightening experience. Focusing on two new entrants called Satyarth and Hari, the film documents their daily routines, which largely revolve around Sanskrit classes. The learning of this ancient script, supposedly to maintain a linguistic tradition, is actually in service of religious dogmatism; in between classes, Guru Avimuktesh continues to preach Islamophobic and casteist ideas, packaged as fact.
Moreover, though fanatically strict on its Hindu teachings, the school pays little attention to the mental and physical wellbeing of the pupils. Scenes of the school’s lavish celebration of its leader’s birthday are intercut with the students’ ramshackle living quarters. Even more shocking than this are the changes we observe in the boys over the course of mere months. Once a fresh-faced youth with a gentle demeanour, Hari soon starts to parrot the guru’s intolerant ideology with terrifying conviction. Laying bare the mechanism of indoctrination, Johar and Kapoor’s film sounds an urgent alarm for a new generation growing up under the spell of extremism.

From former 'street kid' key to South Africa's police corruption inquiry
- Published
The name of controversial businessman Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala has haunted the proceedings of South Africa's major inquiry into alleged police corruption.
The 49-year-old has been accused of supplying generous gifts - including 20 impalas, the weight-loss drug Ozempic and personal loans - to help him buy influence and get police contracts.
In police custody for more than a year in connection with a separate case, Matlala is giving his side of the story before retired Constitutional Court judge Mbuyiseli Madlanga and his panel after an earlier hearing last month was aborted.
The revelations at the Madlanga Commission, in progress for 10 months, have gripped South Africans and they are eager to hear how Matlala responds.
Dressed in a Fendi shirt and Gucci glasses, Matlala did give evidence at a parallel corruption inquiry in parliament last November.
He said he did not know senior police officers and politicians personally and denied corruption allegations though he admitted to having made donations for activities related to the African National Congress (ANC), the main party in the coalition government.
But he has not yet been asked to address the wider allegations made at the Madlanga Commission or the accusation that he was part of a drug trafficking cartel, allegedly known as the Big Five.
Matlala may now be a central figure, but he only came to public prominence three years ago when his name was mentioned in news reports around alleged tender irregularities at a state hospital - though he said he had nothing to do with the tender.
What little is known about his early life is based on what he told parliament last year.
He was born in 1976, when South Africa was still run by a white-minority government, and grew up in a township east of the capital, Pretoria.
He told lawmakers that he was for a time raised by a single mother, who he said then "disappeared on me".
"I had to raise myself. I was actually a street kid," he told lawmakers.
He eventually reunited with his mother in 2002, when she was terminally ill.
After she died, Matlala learned that she had been sexually assaulted, which he said was because of her albinism. Myths surround the condition include people believing that having sex with a woman with the condition would cure the men of illness.
After leaving school, he said he started an informal business to make ends meet, which led to various brushes with the law.
In 2001, he was convicted and served time in prison for the possession of stolen goods.
Over the years, he would be arrested for a string of crimes, including house robberies, a cash-in-transit heist and assault. He denied involvement in them all and was either acquitted or had the charges withdrawn against him.
He told the parliamentary committee that his nickname "Cat" was not, as some had suggested, down to his "nine lives" and ability to survive trouble, but because of his large family - he has nine children with his wife.
But things caught up with him in May 2025 when he was arrested and charged with attempted murder, which he denies. His wife is accused of the same crime and also denies the charge. Unlike her husband, she has been granted bail.
He was later charged with corruption over allegations in relation to providing health services to the police - and last month pleaded guilty as part of a deal with the prosecution but has since withdrawn the plea as the agreement has fallen apart.
He told the parliamentary inquiry last year that he turned his life around in 2017, when he registered his first formal business to provide security services.
Matlala said he later expanded his services into healthcare, and this led to him scoring lucrative contracts, first with a hospital and then the police, even though, as he admitted to lawmakers, he had no track record providing healthcare services.
But since last September, as witnesses gave evidence to the Madlanga Commission, allegations that Matlala had a close and corrupt relationship with senior police officers emerged in the public domain.
This included allegations that the now-suspended Police Minister Senzo Mchunu was indirectly receiving financial campaign money from Matlala to fund his "political endeavours". Mchunu denied these accusations.
Matlala has also been accused of having dealings with Mchunu's predecessor Bheki Cele.
Matlala told parliament's inquiry he had paid Cele a 500,000 rand ($31,000; £23,000) "facilitation fee", which the latter had demanded after police returned firearms seized from Matlala.
The businessman alleged that Cele also made other requests, including asking for help to purchase a home and pay for his son's studies, to which Matlala refused to accede.
Cele admitted to MPs that he had known Matlala for a couple of months and had stayed at his rented penthouse in Pretoria on two occasions but denied receiving money from Matlala.
Matlala's relationship with suspended deputy police chief Maj-Gen Shadrack Sibiya has also come under examination.
Both Matlala and Sibiya denied having a close relationship, insisting their dealings were strictly professional.
But testimony given at the Madlanga Commission painted a different picture.
It was alleged that Sibiya had received 20 impalas from Matlala around the same time Matlala was awarded the police contract. Sibiya denied this, saying he would never "receive anything from a service provider".
A witness also alleged that Matlala had bragged about his "close connections with very senior police officials", including Sibiya, following his arrest in May last year.
Matlala's alleged relationship with other senior police officers have also been brought up at the Madlanga Commission.
Brig Rachel Matjeng, who oversaw the controversial police contract awarded to Matlala, told the commission she had had an on-off romantic relationship with the businessman that included lavish romantic presents – among them shots of Ozempic.
Another senior officer, the head of the police's organised crime unit Maj-Gen Richard Shibiri, admitted to receiving a "personal loan" of $4,000 from Matlala which he repaid.
Shibiri, who oversaw anti-gang, narcotics, illegal mining investigations among others in his role, said the money was for repairs to his son's car. He denied having a close friendship with Matlala, despite speaking to him often and advising him on personal matters.
"At no stage was I aware that he was a member of any cartel or that he was a subject of any criminal investigation," he said.
Shibiri and Matjeng have since been fired from the police force.
Matlala's name was also mentioned in relation to an alleged scandal in Ekurhuleni, a local government area just east of Johannesburg.
It was alleged that while Julius Mkhwanazi was Ekurhuleni's acting police chief, he arranged for blue lights and sirens to be fitted on Matlala's personal vehicles.
Mkhwanazi, who has since been suspended, denied the allegations but did admit to receiving money from Matlala, describing him as a "blood brother" during his appearance at the Madlanga Commission.
The startling revelations that have emerged since September, when the Madlanga Commission began, have left people wondering how such things were allowed to happen.
Many South Africans, anxious to understand the mechanics of the alleged corruption, hope that Matlala has the answers as his testimony continues.

Oslo mayor calls off wedding ceremony after death of Norway's king
- Published
Oslo's Mayor Anne Lindboe has called off her wedding ceremony because of the death of King Harald V of Norway.
The wedding with her fiancé Pål Sandvid was planned to take place on Friday but was postponed after the king died earlier the same day, her political adviser confirmed to the BBC.
"It's hard to imagine an Oslo and a Norway without you. You didn't need a crown to be king," Lindboe wrote in a tribute to the late monarch on Instagram.
Harald reigned for 35 years and died at the national hospital in Norway's capital, where he was being treated for a rare blood condition. His son, King Haakon VIII, ascended the throne on Friday.

After five years together, Lindboe announced the couple's engagement in June this year.
The late king was a popular and reforming leader in Norway who modernised the monarchy.
He broke with tradition by marrying a commoner, Queen Sonja, and served as a unifying figure during Norway's most difficult moments.
Harald died a day before their 58th wedding anniversary.
Members of the public have been gathering to lay flowers at a memorial outside the Royal Palace in Oslo.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a televised memorial address that his country was "united in grief and gratitude" for Harald's service and that his "legacy lives on".

Noting that a student’s talent is not diminished simply because they did not manage to secure expected marks in an examination, Bihar Education Minister Mithilesh Tiwari announced on Friday (August 28, 2026) that the word “fail” would be replaced with “eligible for skills” in marksheets of students appearing for Class 10 and 12 board exams in the State.
Mr. Tiwari also added that the State Education Department would soon issue the “necessary directives” to the Bihar School Examination Board (BSEB) in this regard.
“Students taking the Class 10 board supplementary examinations will receive special classes for one month to help them prepare better and to ensure success”, Mr. Tiwari said.
“The State government wants to protect the morale of students and an exam score does not define a child’s overall talent or future potential. So, the Bihar [School] Examination Board would use the word “kaushal ke liye patra” (eligible for skills) instead of “fail” on their marksheets”, said Mr. Tiwari while adding, “the Education Department would amend the rules and issue directives to the Bihar School Examination Board soon in this regard.
The Minister’s announcement was welcomed by students appearing for Class 12 examination, which is expected to be held in February 2027.
“Yes, change of the word will have a bigger role in maintaining our morale... ‘fail’ is such a demeaning term. Because of the social taboo attached with it, many students had, earlier, even taken their own life upon seeing the word on their school certificates, but now the government is taking steps to ensure students’ well-being . The move is a big boost”, said a group of students outside a coaching institute in Kankerbagh, Patna, on Friday (August 28, 2026).
Earlier, the Bihar government had announced it will conduct the Teacher Recruitment Examination-4 in a single phase following which students called off their protest in Patna’s Gardanibagh. The students were holding agitations over alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations. While expressing satisfaction over the government’s announcement, the students said “since the government has agreed to their demands, they have called off their ongoing protest... there is no point in taking this protest further”.
Student initiatives
Meanwhile, Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary will be launching a “Teacher Support Portal” at an event to mark Teachers’ Day on September 5, under which one teacher from each district would be honoured with a State-level award. Earlier, on August 27, the State government had launched a 24-hour one-on-one interactive learning digital platform, “Bihar Vidya Saathi” for students from Classes 9 to 12 offering live access to teachers and digital study materials to the students.
The announcement by the government further said that around 75,000 teachers would provide one-on-one academic support round the clock, allowing students to choose teachers as per their requirements.
Mr. Choudhary had also launched a platform for 700 Saraswati Vidya Niketan Model schools across the State through video conferencing on August 27. “It is a significant initiative towards providing quality education and proper guidance to children. Students will also have AI-powered tools for conceptual learning, unlimited study and practice, and digital material for Bihar Board, JEE and NEET examination preparations”, said a government press release.

From ant bites and medicines to dust and pollen, allergies affect millions of Indians. While for many they are merely a tiresome nuisance, in some cases routine exposures can turn into life-threatening crises.
What began as routine health issues for three Chennai residents spiralled into prolonged medical ordeals, underscoring the unpredictable and sometimes life-threatening nature of allergies. Experts note that there is a need for better awareness about them to enable early diagnosis, as well as a need for more research in the Indian context into allergies and their triggers.
What patients experience
R. Neelakandan of Minjur underwent open-heart surgery in 2017. During his recovery, he developed persistent rashes after taking a prescribed medicine. His cardiologist referred him to a dermatologist, but even after two years of treatment, the condition showed little improvement. He was eventually advised to take monthly injections costing ₹19,000 each.
Relief came unexpectedly — through an autorickshaw driver.
“The driver took me to a doctor in Chennai who, he said, had treated him successfully,” Mr. Neelakandan recalls. “The doctor realised that I was allergic to a drug, and changed the medicine that I have to take regularly to another one. Earlier, I was spending nearly ₹25,000 a month on treatment and I felt I was a burden to my family. Now, my costs have come down to less than ₹2,000.”
For schoolteacher H. Deepalakshmi, what should have been a simple ant bite turned into a near-fatal emergency. Her blood pressure plummeted, she became dizzy and semi-conscious, and she had to be rushed to hospital. “After the first incident nine years ago, I started carrying the doctor’s prescription with me at all times,” says the 52-year-old. “Three years later, I was bitten again. I immediately showed the prescription at the hospital and received the injection. The symptoms were milder the second time and even less severe the third time.” Her doctor later explained that certain ant bites can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.
Rohini Karupiah, a college professor, has battled wheezing since childhood. During severe attacks she required oxygen support at home. Her bronchial allergy, she says, runs in the family. “My father and his sister both had wheezing, but my condition was much more severe,” she says.
While the triggers in these cases were very different, specialists say they reflect the broad spectrum of allergic disorders that affect millions of Indians.
More than a rash
‘Allergy’ is an umbrella term covering a range of immune-system responses. Symptoms can vary from mild skin rashes and itching to breathing difficulties and life-threatening anaphylactic shock. Allergic rhinitis — commonly triggered by dust, pollen and other airborne particles — is among the most widespread forms of allergy. Specialists, however, also encounter less common triggers, including insect bites, medications and substances that the body may have tolerated previously.
Chennai-based allergy specialist R. Sridharan says allergies can affect virtually every system in the body. “People can be allergic to mould, pollen, nuts, sunlight — even ant bites,” he explains. “Allergies may appear as skin rashes or hives, or manifest as allergic rhinitis. They can progress to sinus disease and, in some cases, bronchial asthma as well.”
According to Dr. Sridharan, allergic reactions are most often mediated by Immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies produced by white blood cells. Once the immune system identifies a substance as harmful, it may react aggressively whenever it encounters it. The reaction triggers the release of histamine, which dilates blood vessels and increases tissue permeability.
“The person feels hot, blood pressure can drop, and in severe cases the patient can go into shock,” he says. “Histamines cause swelling, warmth and itching. Treatment focuses on countering these effects.”
A growing concern
The scale of the problem is significant.
In their study, ‘Epidemiology of Allergic Rhinitis in India: A Systematic Review’, published in the International Journal of Academic Medicine and Pharmacy in 2023, researchers V. Sundararaman and A. Sathish Ponni estimated that nearly one in six people in Tamil Nadu may suffer from allergic rhinitis. The researchers noted that allergic rhinitis is a major public-health concern across India, although its prevalence varies widely across regions. Geography, climate, air quality and lifestyle factors all influence the incidence and severity of allergic disorders.
Allergies may be triggered by pollen, fungal spores and food items ranging from grains such as rice and wheat to legumes, chickpeas and vegetables. Increasing urbanisation, environmental pollution and changing lifestyles are also believed to be contributing to the rising burden of allergic disease.
Need for better research
Dr. Sridharan says eosinophil counts play an important role in identifying allergies. Common diagnostic tools include nasal smear and sputum eosinophil tests, ELISA tests to identify specific IgE antibodies and Phadiatop tests to detect inhalant allergies. Skin tests may also be used to pinpoint specific triggers. He cites research from the United States showing that some people who believed they were allergic to apples were actually reacting to birch pollen present on the fruit.
Despite the growing prevalence of allergic disorders, experts say India still relies heavily on treatment protocols adapted from Western populations.
In their paper, ‘An Appraisal of Allergic Disorders in India and an Urgent Call for Action’, published in the World Allergy Organization Journal in 2020, Mamidipudi Thirumala Krishna and colleagues argued that current management protocols are largely based on international guidelines developed using Western data. They noted a shortage of robust real-world studies assessing how well these approaches apply to Indian patients.
As the experiences of Neelakandan, Deepalakshmi and Rohini demonstrate, allergies are far more than seasonal irritants. Left undiagnosed or poorly managed, they can become chronic, debilitating and, at times, life-threatening conditions. For doctors and patients alike, identifying the trigger remains the first and most critical step.
(R. Sujatha is an independent journalist based in Chennai. sujatha.raghunath@gmail.com)

Although India could only manage an eighth-place finish after a 3-4 penalty shootout loss, it showed fight to twice claw back from being a goal down to hold Belgium 3-3 in Wavre at the Belifus Arena on Friday.
At 2-2, veteran midfielder Manpreet Singh was struck near his eye as he put his body on the line to get on the end of Hugo Labouchere’s close-range shot. A bloodied Manpreet was helped off the pitch to a round of applause from the home crowd. But even as the Indian team could recover from the horror injury, Belgium pounced on an error to score through Nicolas de Kerpel.
The goal was upheld despite India’s referral for a touch on the body in the buildup, which added to a frustratingly mixed afternoon for skipper Harmanpreet Singh.
AS IT HAPPENED | India vs Belgium Highlights
In the first quarter, he was the recipient of a five-minute suspension for an embarrassing situation when his side fielded 12 players before being handed a green card in the third.
But in between them, he struck with his trademark powerful dragpushes to twice equalise, with the second one coming with just seconds left on the clock to level the scores.
However, he couldn’t find a way past Vincent Vanasch in the shootout, as did his teammate Sukhjeet Singh. India goalkeeper Mohith HS committed too early as Belgium managed to find the net four times in the shootout to end its home World Cup with something to cheer about.
Despite looking second best for better part of the game, India’s fight cannot be faulted after a torrid World Cup campaign. India silenced the home side within six minutes into the start when Abhishek Nain’s shot deflected in off Alexander Hendrickx for the opening goal.
But Belgium continued to suffocate India with its full court press and launched a barrage of shots. While Suraj Karkera resisted in the opening quarter, Mohith couldn’t stop an unmarked Roman Duvekot from equalising before Labouchere scored from Belgium’s fifth Penalty Corner.
India found some much-needed control in the third quarter to limit Belgium from penetrating its circle, while coming close to scoring from open play. But yet again, it needed inspiration from Harmanpreet in set-pieces to save its blushes.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on Sunday (August 23, 2026) said that the Influenza A (H1N1) viruses currently circulating in the country belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. It clarified that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic.
“These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1, and have been in circulation since 2025. The Influenza strains currently circulating are also well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere,” ICMR said. “Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting,” it added.
Common symptoms of the illness include fever, cough, headache, and body ache, and most people recover with appropriate care and rest. However, young children, elderly persons, and individuals with underlying medical conditions may be at a greater risk of complications. If symptoms persist, worsen, or become severe, consultation with a doctor is advised, it said.
The Union Health Ministry has said that it is closely monitoring the situation through regular surveillance and is undertaking necessary public health measures.
India has registered a rise in seasonal Influenza A(H1N1) cases, commonly called swine flu, this monsoon, especially in major cities. Delhi has reported 1,777 confirmed H1N1 cases so far this year, including 114 new cases on August 20. Karnataka has registered over 4,000 cases, with more than half reported from Bengaluru. Rising influenza activity has also been reported in Mumbai, Chennai and parts of Kerala.
National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) data show that H1N1 activity was relatively low in 2021 (778 cases, 12 deaths) after the pandemic period, but rebounded sharply in 2022 (13,202 cases, 410 deaths) and remained substantial in 2023 (8,125 cases, 129 deaths). By June 2024, India had already recorded 7,215 cases and 150 deaths, and year-end numbers were higher. NCDC’s 2025 reporting shows that H1N1 continued to circulate across multiple States.
NCDC maintains a nationwide influenza surveillance network and publishes State-wise data and H1N1 treatment/prevention guidelines. It recommends seasonal influenza vaccination based on WHO strain recommendations. For the 2025–26 season, India’s recommended trivalent vaccine included H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria components, with circulating Indian H1N1 strains aligning with vaccine strains.
“People at higher risk should consider annual vaccination and seek medical advice promptly if flu symptoms become severe,” Anil Bansal of the Delhi Medical Association said.

How England are building an attack to trouble Australia
- Published
Exciting or too early to say?
Any praise for England's pace attack this summer comes with the caveat of the quality of Pakistan's batting - and the fact they are operating in helpful home conditions.
But, after having their hand forced by the retirement of Ben Stokes, England have stumbled on something encouraging.
A four-man pace attack of Ollie Robinson, Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson, who dismissed Pakistan for 110 on day two of the second Test at Lord's, appears potent and, perhaps crucially for the future, are complementing each other in different ways...
- Sarfaraz denies knowing about Pakistan threat to end tour 
  - Published2 hours ago
No longer a need for speed
After the first-Test win at Headingley, captain Joe Root said his pace bowlers "do not know how good they can be" and praised the variety they offer.
Root suggested this group is ahead of bowling stocks from his previous stint as captain, when he often called upon right-arm seamers James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Chris Woakes and Ben Stokes, in terms of their variation.
The most obvious differential between his new quartet is pace - something brought into further focus by England's decision to prioritise bowlers who reach high speeds during last winter's Ashes defeat.
While Archer was touching 95mph in the quickest opening spell of his career on day two at Lord's, Robinson was operating around 78mph at the other end.
Tongue's average pace across the series is actually higher than Archer, though Archer has bowled a higher percentage of his deliveries over 90mph.
Atkinson slots in just below Tongue and Archer, who joked he could play until he is 40 given how his team-mates are sharing the load.
"It is a good attack," said former England captain Michael Vaughan. "They can all get better and that is a really good sign.
"This batting line-up is possibly the easiest I have seen to bowl to but this attack, bowling the way they are doing, will challenge better batting line-ups.
"They will challenge the Australia line-up quite nicely if they bowl like this."
Robinson the metronome
What Robinson has lacked in pace, he is making up for with skill. Four more wickets on Friday took him to 17 wickets at an average of 8.84 across his three Tests this summer.
Helped by lively English pitches, Robinson has been able to concentrate on his greatest skill - his control of line and length.
Against Pakistan, he has hit a good length with 70% of his deliveries. Atkinson has the next best record with 52%.
It has meant Robinson has been relentlessly testing the defences of Pakistan's batters, while giving them few bad balls to hit.
He bowled 31 deliveries in a row without conceding a run on Friday and 13 overs, which cost only 11 runs, were the most economical figures by a pace bowler bowling 10 overs or more in England for 13 years.
"Ollie Robinson is an extraordinarily skillful bowler," said Vaughan.
"[England] are trying to get him to 81mph more consistently and if he can get to that he will challenge all batting line-ups in all conditions.
"He has been the tone-setter we were crying out for in the winter."
1 of 2
Similar but different
England's 2005 pace attack of Stephen Harmison, Andrew Flintoff, Matthew Hoggard and Simon Jones is their best in terms of its all-round threat.
Harmison and Flintoff provided pace and bounce, Jones the skiddier threat and Hoggard genuine swing.
While Robinson and Archer can operate as swing bowlers as well as bowling their more natural seam, this current group's variety comes more from their plans and their specific characteristics.
Archer and Robinson have particularly high release points, while Tongue delivers the ball from notably wide on the crease - 96.4cm from the stumps compared with Archer's 40.3cm - with his unusual, beyond-the-perpendicular action.
Atkinson, who took 34 wickets at 20.17 in his first year in Test cricket in 2024, is the all-rounder who bowls accurately, but does so at a higher pace than Robinson.
"You want a bowler who can swing it, another bowler who has proper pace, another who can reverse swing it and another who can do the donkey work," said BBC chief cricket commentator Jonathan Agnew.
"It is a well-balanced attack but without the spinner."
Tongue targets the timbers
Archer's natural angle makes him particularly effective against left-handers.
He averages 23.9 against southpaws compared with 31.3 against right-handers - helpful for England because Tongue and Atkinson's records are almost a mirror image.
Tongue averages 21.5 against right-handers but 35.7 against lefties. Atkinson's record is 19.9 compared with 31.7.
Tongue's position on the crease also aids him in his speciality of targeting the stumps.
Across this series, 22% of Tongue's deliveries would have hit the timbers while a figure of 29% at Headingley, where he took eight wickets across the first Test, was the highest by an England bowler in a home Test for 15 years.
And after two more wickets on Friday, Tongue's bowling strike-rate now stands at a dismissal once every 39.8 balls, putting him 12th on the list of bowlers to have taken 30 Test wickets.
"Tongue is the one who is really developing the best of them," Agnew said.
A home Ashes series is less than one year away. England's bowlers appear to be shaping up nicely.

Nvidia is reportedly moving forward to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The acquisition could help the hardware giant expand and fortify its deep integration with the wider AI industry.
Among other things, Hugging Face is a cloud repository for AI models, similar in some respects to what GitHub is for conventional computer software. The deal is not finalized, so it could still run into trouble ahead, but both parties appear to be actively pursuing it, according to a report from The Information, which cites one person with knowledge of the matter. Another source confirmed to CNBC that talks are underway.

4 ways to cope with constant thoughts about your body image
In the age of weight loss drugs, Instagram face and an endless scroll of Facetuned bodies, it can be difficult to love how your body looks.
But what if you could change the way you think about your body?
Life Kit
How to stop fixating on your body in the era of GLP-1s
Psychologist Diana Hill, a specialist in acceptance and commitment therapy, helps her clients practice mental exercises rooted in "body image flexibility." It's a term from the field of psychology that describes the ability to cope with uncomfortable feelings about your looks.
Body image flexibility doesn't require you to love how your body looks, or even feel neutral about it. It's more about what you do when you have negative thoughts about it.
"How much energy and time are you putting into obsessing about [your looks] in the mirror versus engaging in your life and the things you care about?" Hill says.
Hill, co-author of ACT Daily Journal: Get Unstuck and Live Fully with Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, shares exercises to help you stay present — and deal with the very real pressures we face to obsess about and alter our appearance.
Focus your attention inward
When you look in the mirror and all you can see is your nose, belly, acne or wrinkles, practice flexible attention. That means being mindful of negative thoughts about body image — and redirecting them.
One way to do this, Hill suggests, is to turn your attention to what's happening inside your body instead. Think about all the things your internal organs are doing right now. Are you hungry or full? Does your stomach feel tense or relaxed? Are you feeling nervous? Excited? Happy? Calm?
"It's what we call 'interoceptive awareness,'" Hill says. "It's associated with benefits like better ability to pay attention to hunger and fullness, and better empathy and interpersonal awareness."
Appreciate what your body can do
You can also turn your attention outward by focusing on your body's functionality, Hill says. Ask yourself: How are you using your body at this moment?
You might say, "Right now, I'm sitting on the floor. My eyes are seeing a tree," Hill says. Then take a moment to appreciate those physical abilities. "My eyes may not always be able to see a tree the way I can see a tree now. My ears are receiving sounds. My body is breathing in air. These are ways in which my body is connecting me to this world."
Interrogate your intentions
If you're uncomfortable with a body part, say, your stomach, and are in the habit of sucking it in to make it appear smaller, take a moment to notice that behavior, Hill says. Then, ask yourself some questions.
- Are there times when you're sucking your stomach in more — or less? "There may be times when you let it go a little bit because you feel safer. Maybe you're alone on a hike or in bed," Hill says.
- Is how you feel about your stomach based on a message you've received from culture and society? "Is that messaging [what] you want to believe and let guide your life?" Hill says.
- How do your feelings about your stomach affect your daily life? "Are you less comfortable in your clothes? Are you distracted? Are you not standing up and speaking in front of a group?" Hill says.
This exercise may help you see that "there's a whole slew of things that are happening at the biological level, the psychological level and the social level," Hill says, that leads us to "just automatically shut off a part of our body."
Do an energy audit
"Get honest about how much time and effort is going into your body and where it's taking energy from your life," says Hill. Maybe you're spending a lot of time posting selfies for likes on Instagram, or buying beauty products.
Then ask yourself: What fuels your energy in relationship with your body? "Maybe it's being outside, doing movement you enjoy or playing with your dog," Hill says.
Swap some of the time you spend focusing on your image with another activity that helps you enjoy your body.
"Every little bit of energy you're putting into sucking in your stomach or [feeling] distracted by your shiny face pulls away energy from you," Hill says — your creative force, your ability to connect and your talents. "And what people want is you."

Squint, or strabismus, is a condition in which the eyes are not aligned and do not look in the same direction at the same time. One eye may turn inwards towards the nose (esotropia), outwards (exotropia), upwards or downwards, while the other eye remains focused on an object. This misalignment may be constant or may occur intermittently, such as when a person is tired.
A recent study estimated that horizontal strabismus affects 1.81% of the global population, or about 138.5 million people. Exotropia affects an estimated 1.14% (87.5 million), compared with 0.67% (60 million) for esotropia. The pattern has also shifted across generations, with exotropia now more common globally. The study found regional differences, but noted that parts of South Asia remain under-represented in research.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises strabismus as one of the eye conditions that can require long-term monitoring and treatment. WHO’s guidance on vision screening in preschool children notes that strabismus is one of the causes of amblyopia, or reduced vision resulting from abnormal visual development.
What are the signs and symptoms?
The most obvious sign is that the eyes appear to point in different directions. Some children may close one eye in bright light, tilt or turn their head to see, or have difficulty judging distances.
Children may not always complain about poor vision. When the eyes are misaligned, the brain can suppress the image from the affected eye to avoid double vision. If this happens during the period when vision is developing, the child can develop amblyopia, commonly called lazy eye.
Adults who develop a squint may experience double vision, blurred vision, eye strain, headaches or difficulty with depth perception. A new squint that appears suddenly in an adult should be assessed promptly because it can sometimes be associated with conditions affecting the eye muscles, nerves or brain.
Not every apparent squint is true strabismus. Some children appear to have crossed eyes because of the shape of the eyelids or the bridge of the nose. This is known as pseudostrabismus and can be distinguished from true strabismus through an eye examination.
What causes a squint?
Strabismus occurs when the systems that control eye movement and alignment do not work properly together. The problem may involve the eye muscles, the nerves that control them, or the parts of the brain that coordinate eye movements.
In many children, the exact cause is not known. Genetic factors can play a role, and children with a family history of strabismus are at higher risk.
Refractive errors can also contribute. Squint is also more common in children with certain neurological or developmental conditions. Being born prematurely or with low birth weight are recognised risk factors.
In adults, strabismus can develop due to conditions such as diabetes, thyroid eye disease, stroke, neurological disorders or trauma. Poor vision in one eye can also affect the alignment of the eyes.
How is a squint diagnosed?
An ophthalmologist usually examines how the eyes are aligned and how they move together. The assessment may include measuring visual acuity in each eye, checking for refractive errors and examining how the eyes respond when one eye is covered and uncovered.
In children, the examination is also aimed at identifying amblyopia and determining whether the child has developed binocular vision normally.
Further tests may be needed when the squint develops suddenly, is associated with double vision or is accompanied by other neurological or eye symptoms.
What are the treatment options?
Treatment depends on the type and cause of the squint, the age of the person, how frequently the eye turns and whether vision in either eye has been affected. Glasses are often the first treatment when a refractive error contributes to the misalignment. In accommodative esotropia, correcting long-sightedness can substantially reduce the inward turning of the eyes.
If a child has amblyopia, it may have to be treated as well.
Some types of strabismus may benefit from specific eye exercises, though these are not suitable for every type. Surgery may be needed when glasses and other treatments do not adequately correct the misalignment. It involves adjusting selected eye muscles to improve alignment.
Early treatment can reduce the impact of amblyopia and support binocular vision.
Early assessment, especially for persistent misalignment or squint in a young child, can identify refractive errors, amblyopia or other problems and help determine whether observation, glasses, amblyopia treatment or surgery is needed.

Quick Answer
PowerShell commands such as Get-Help, Get-Command, Get-Process, Start-Process, Stop-Process, Get-Service, Stop-Service, Get-Content, Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, Move-Item, Remove-Item, and Set-Location help you manage apps, services, files, folders, and system tasks faster on Windows.
PowerShell is a Windows program that simplifies system administration. You can use it to perform many system tasks efficiently and automate repetitive ones. However, to do either, you must know the right commands, or cmdlets (command-lets), as PowerShell calls them.
A typical PowerShell cmdlet follows the verb-noun structure, where the noun is the object you want to act on, and the verb is the action you want to perform on it. This makes them predictable and easy to remember.
Here’s a quick reference guide covering all the essential Windows PowerShell commands to help you get started with PowerShell.
Table of Contents
Essential PowerShell Commands for Windows
Get-Help
Get-Help is a handy cmdlet you can use any time you want to learn about a PowerShell concept or command. It shows information for everything from cmdlets and functions to aliases and scripts. Plus, it shows the exact syntax along with all the available parameters to eliminate the need for guesswork.
Syntax:
Get-Help
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Help cmdlet:
- Get-Help Get-Process : Find out what the Get-Process command does
- Get-Help Get-Process -Detailed : Get a detailed description for the Get-Process cmdlet
- Get-Help Get-Process -Online : View a detailed explanation of the command with examples on Microsoft’s official documentation online
If Get-Help doesn’t return any result, try updating it by running:
Update-Help
Get-Command
Get-Command lists all executable commands installed on your computer, including cmdlets, aliases (or shortcuts that point to other commands), and functions (snippets or scripts that perform specific actions). It’s useful when you want to make sure the command you’re trying to use is supported by PowerShell and available on your system.
Syntax:
Get-Command
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Command -ListImported : Get a list of all commands in the current session
- Get-Command Get-AppLockerPolicy : View information about the Get-AppLockerPolicy cmdlet
- Get-Command -CommandType Alias : List all alias-type executables
- Get-Command *Service* : Get all the service-related executable elements on your system
Get-Process
Get-Process returns a table of all operating system processes (apps or executables) running on your computer locally. For each item in the table, you see the process name, ID, CPU consumption, and a few other details. This makes it really easy to identify which process is consuming significantly more resources, so you can act on it accordingly and free up system resources.
Syntax:
Get-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Process cmdlet:
- Get-Process -Name notepad : Get details about the Notepad process
- Get-Process explorer | Format-List * : Display detailed information about the explorer processes, including all its properties and their values
Stop-Process
Stop-Process allows you to stop one or more running processes on your computer right from the PowerShell window. To use it, you need the process name or the process ID (or PID), which you can identify by running the Get-Process command.
Syntax:
Stop-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Process cmdlet:
- Stop-Process -Name notepad : Close the Notepad app
- Stop-Process -Name notepad -F : Force close Notepad
- Stop-Process -Id 3380 : Close the app with a PID of 3380
Start-Process
Start-Process is a PowerShell command that lets you launch one or more processes (or apps) on your computer. You can even open an executable file using it. Start-Process also gives you the ability to choose how you want to start a process. For instance, you may start a program as an administrator or open specific files with their default apps.
Syntax:
Start-Process
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Start-Process cmdlet:
- Start-Process notepad.exe : Launch the Notepad app
- Start-Process -FilePath “notepad” -Wait -WindowStyle Maximized : Open Notepad in a maximized window
- Start-Process -FilePath “sort.exe” : Start a process that uses the sort.exe file
- Start-Process -FilePath “powershell” -Verb RunAs : Open PowerShell as an administrator
Get-Service
Get-Service retrieves and gives you the status of all Windows services running on your computer. It’s useful when you want to identify the status of background services.
Syntax:
Get-Service
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Command cmdlet:
- Get-Service -Name wuauserv : Check the status of the Windows Update service
- Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Running"} : Filter services to only view the ones that are currently running
Stop-Service
The Stop-Service PowerShell cmdlet lets you stop a system service. You’d typically use it after you’ve run the Get-Service command and identified the problematic service running in the background.
Syntax:
Stop-Service -Name
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Stop-Service cmdlet:
- Stop-Service -Name wuauserv : Stop the Windows Update service
- Stop-Service -DisplayName “telnet” | Stop-Service : Stop a service using its display name
- Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force : Stop the Spooler service along with other dependent services
Get-Content
Get-Content helps you read the contents of an item within the PowerShell window. You’d mostly use it to get the contents of a file. All you need to do is specify the file and its location. You can even mention the number of lines in the file you want to read, among other things.
Syntax:
Get-Content -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-Content cmdlet:
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -TotalCount 10 : Read only the first ten lines of the file
- Get-Content -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Wait : Monitor a file and display new lines as they’re added and the file is saved
Get-ChildItem
The Get-ChildItem cmdlet allows you to view all the items (files and folders) at your specified location. Running it without any parameters returns items in your current location, but you can force it to find items at other locations, too.
Syntax:
Get-ChildItem -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Get-ChildItem cmdlet:
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test : Find files and folders in the Test folder in the D: directory
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Name : Get the names of files and folders at a specified location
- Get-ChildItem -Path D:\Test -Filter *.txt -Recurse : Scan a directory and its folders for all text files
Copy-Item
Copy-Item lets you copy items (files and folders) from one location to another. You just need to specify the path of the file or folder you want to move along with the path of the location where you want to move it. The copied file continues to live at the original location.
Syntax:
Copy-Item -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Copy-Item cmdlet:
- Copy-Item D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Copy sample.txt file to another location with sample2.txt name
- Copy-Item D:\Test\ -Destination D:\Test2\ -Recurse : Duplicate the Test folder along with all its subfolders and files to Test2
Move-Item
Move-Item is a handy cmdlet for when you want to move an item (file or folder) from one location to another. Unlike the copy command, it doesn’t keep the item at its original location after the operation. Instead, it moves it to the new location.
Syntax:
Move-Item -Path -Destination
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Move-Item cmdlet:
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\ : Move the sample.txt file from the Test folder to the Test2 folder
- Move-Item -Path D:\Test\sample.txt -Destination D:\Test2\sample2.txt : Move the sample.txt file to the Test2 folder and rename it to sample2.txt
- Move-Item -Path .\*.txt -Destination D:\Test2 : Move all files with the .txt extension in the current directory to Test2
Remove-Item
Remove-Item allows you to remove or delete one or more items (files and folders) from a location. Remember that this cmdlet permanently deletes the item instead of moving it to the Recycle Bin for restoration.
Syntax:
Remove-Item -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Remove-Item cmdlet:
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a dot (.) in their name
- Remove-Item -Path D:\Test*.* : Delete all files with a .doc file extension in the Test folder
Set-Location
Set-Location lets you change the current working location to your specified location. It’s quite handy when you’ve to perform multiple operations on different directories.
Syntax:
Set-Location -Path
Example use cases for PowerShell’s Set-Location cmdlet:
- Set-Location -Path D: : Set the working location to the D: drive
- Set-Location -Path D: -PassThru : Set the working location to the D: drive and display that location
You Should Also Learn Command Prompt
PowerShell is just one of the many powerful tools Microsoft bundles with Windows. You also have Command Prompt (CMD) — a command-line interpreter that lets you perform various system operations using commands. If you haven’t already, be sure to check out our essential Command Prompt commands cheatsheet, as that can help you use your Windows PC more efficiently as well.

There is much to be said for the extraordinary women living ordinary lives, who nonetheless shaped India. Women have changed public life in the country far more than their presence in formal politics would suggest.
And so, as India marked its 79th birthday over the weekend, I found myself reflecting on the multitude of people’s movements, big and small – as well as the women who helped shape them. During India’s struggle for freedom from British rule, women organised boycotts of British goods, made contraband salt and marched to confront the police, taking on roles usually dominated by men. In the 1970s Chipko movement, protesting deforestation, women put their bodies on the line, wrapping them around trees to stop them being felled, turning a local struggle into a national reckoning over environment and development. More recently, grandmothers in Shaheen Bagh sat to protest the citizenship law, which critics have denounced as discriminatory, creating space for dissent when many thought none existed.
Today, routes into public life for women have multiplied, with social media enabling people without political links to be in the public eye. But not all barriers have disappeared. Electoral politics remains notoriously hard to break into, especially for women. Almost half of all female parliamentarians and state legislators come from political families, while for men it is 18%, a 2025 analysis by Association for Democratic Reforms showed.
What makes a woman leading an ordinary life suddenly want to put her head above the parapet to change things for everyone? I spoke to women thrust into the spotlight in the recent student movement, who have stepped in front of vans, starved themselves and had abuse hurled at them in the process – to find out why they do it.
‘Politics is not just slogans and protests’: Neha Bora, 29
The president of the leftwing All India Students’ Association, Bora fasted for 23 days, demanding accountability over exam paper leaks and the resignation of the Education Minister during the Cockroach Protests. Now, she is touring the country as part of a Gen Z Rising outreach campaign on education reforms.
“I am a PhD student at Jawaharlal Nehru University in theatre and performance studies. My family’s political understanding is very different from mine. I ended up joining politics because that was the only way I could make sense of the times that I was living in – to not be … completely helpless in the decisions that are made for me, that should be made by me. To have a say in what I do, how I do it and what gets done around me. What is tolerable, what is good, what is injustice – all these definitions made sense to me through politics. Theatre was the first thing that taught me that politics is not just slogans and protests. Politics is the very language in which you talk to yourselves, the thoughts you formulate in your head, the relationships you have with your friends, family and peers. Student politics reaffirmed this idea.
Freedom as a student means the ability to study in a university where the model of education has not been turned into an opportunity for profit. Where education is something that helps societies move forward from dogmatism, conservatism and orthodoxy.”
‘Freedom for me is to have a voice – and not be ashamed’: Rhiya Ahir, 27
A model, actor and theatre artist from Mumbai, Ahir made the split-second decision to physically block a police van holding detained protesters – an act that exposed her to an organised hate campaign.
“I started doing theatre when I was four and a half. It taught me empathy and understanding other people’s pain, even people I don’t know. I’ve always been raised with the belief that if you see something wrong you have to step in.
Freedom for me is to have a voice, to put it across confidently and to not be ashamed. I was trolled for a photo in a swimsuit. But what about the uncles who wear chaddis at the Ganga ghat? My clothes are not my character. My clothes cannot overshadow the point or the fact that I was there, and I helped 20 students get back home safely that day. So, my clothes are just my clothes.
The hate did make me second-guess myself. The first two days [after the Mumbai protest] were very difficult because I was still trying to wrap my head around what had happened. They couldn’t find fault with my argument, so they started questioning my character. They went through my Instagram and found that I was a model. They talked about what I wear. They said she’s doing it for the camera.
When the hate started pouring in I was like, ‘What did I do to offend someone? Did I do something wrong?’ Then I realised this doesn’t change my reality. This doesn’t change who I am as a person. I don’t have to prove myself to anyone.”
‘The police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me’: Danish Ali, 24
Ali was among the student activists on hunger strike at Jantar Mantar. A member of the Jawaharlal Nehru University student union, she faces a year-long suspension for dismantling a facial recognition system at the campus library. For her, freedom is deeply personal and rooted in her identity as a Muslim woman.
“I come from a very small town in Madhya Pradesh. No one in my family had even visited the city, so going to Delhi for higher education was almost like going abroad for education. Since the protest, the police have visited my ancestral village asking for information on me. They called my father, asking him to tell me to focus on my studies.
As a student activist, freedom means to be able to critique the government openly and say that we don’t like their policies. Freedom is being assertive about your individuality and not caring what the society would says, what your parents might say or what the state might do to you.
Freedom also means being an equal citizen in this country. Muslims in this country are being made to feel as if they are secondary and that they don’t have any right to express their religious or cultural identities. I am an equal citizen and I don’t want anyone to tell me otherwise.”
‘What used to work … won’t work with the youth’: Ratna Singh, 31
She traded a career in the law and journalism to join the Cockroach Janata party, where she now serves as the legal head. She felt drawn to the protests, seeing her work reflected in the students’ demand for accountability. Initially hesitant to become its public face, she stepped forward as spokesperson when they needed female voices.
“When I was in law school, most of my classmates would go to law chambers for internships but I would spend the summers teaching children at NGOs. Education has been something I have been very sensitive towards, and I believe every child should have access to it.
A lot of people were criticising us [and calling us] an impatient generation. We are impatient because we want to see change. We can’t be protesting and be OK with not getting answers from the government. We are also just done with divide and rule politics on the basis of religion. Political parties need to understand that what used to work for a certain mindset of people – it won’t work with the youth.
There are so many protests which have begun in different parts of the country. The fear of speaking up is gone. We are seeing a lot of leaders coming up in their own districts. They are starting their own initiatives. I think that’s giving us all hope to keep going.”
What else we’re reading about
Political promises | In his Independence Day speech, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a series of youth-focused initiatives, including an AI skills programme, free online coaching for competitive exams and a countrywide sport talent hunt. His call to identify “dimagi naxals”, or people aligned with Naxal ideology, referring to the armed guerilla movement in central India, was criticised by the Opposition as a threat to suppress critics and rivals.
Environment targets missed | The Green India Mission, for protecting and restoring the country’s declining forest cover, fell short of its target by 97% over the past decade, according to an audit report tabled in Parliament. New forest cover added was just 0.03409 million hectares, the report said, citing poor planning and inadequate funding.
Sister act | Two women of Indian origin adopted by separate Dutch families 40 years ago, who became friends as children, recently discovered they are sisters after a DNA test, Reuters reported. “It’s like a missing puzzle piece has been found,” one said.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Actor Imran Khan (@imrankhan) recommends: “Rang De Basanti is an extremely timely and relevant film for this moment; it follows a young English film-maker who befriends a group of Indian students. They set out to make a film about the Indian freedom movement. A tragic accident blurs the lines between past and present, throwing them into their own conflict against an unjust power structure. The film is funny but also heartbreaking. It celebrates the spirit of the great revolutionaries, and imagines what their modern counterparts might stand for. And the soundtrack gives us AR Rahman at his most audaciously experimental. It rocks.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
Two
Question hour in Lok Sabha functioned for 1% percent of its scheduled time during the parliament’s monsoon session, the lowest since 2019, according to PRS Legislative Research, a nonprofit that tracks the functioning of the parliament and state assemblies. The key forum for members of parliament to question the government saw two questions answered in nine minutes, PRS said.
Vibe check
For creator Maroof Umar (@maroofculmen), storytelling can change the way we see the world. And the stories he tells, rooted in heritage and culture through cinematically shot videos, can both break and mend your heart. Each has a person at its center but the stories also belong to the city and its communities. His short videos capture his (and my) hometown of Lucknow most frequently, but his latest work takes us to a sweet shop in Varanasi. In it, Ram Bhandar makes tricolor treats in a nod to the colors of the Indian flag, carrying on a tradition begun by his ancestors decades before, as they tried to spread patriotic fervor during the freedom movement.

The auspicious Raksha Bandhan festival which celebrates brother-sister bond is observed on the full moon of the Hindu month of Shravana. This year, it is being celebrated on 28 August, Friday. Symbolizing the bond of protection, harmony, mutual respect, a sense of responsibility towards one another and celebrating the enduring love between siblings, sisters tie rakhi around their brothers’ right wrists on this day. Rakhi is a sacred thread symbolic of well-being, prosperity and long life.
As a part of tradition, Brothers in exchange of rakhi give gifts to their sisters and pledge to stand by and protect them through life’s challenges. The significance of vibrant celebrations extends beyond biological siblings. Even cousins, friends and neighbours exchange rakhis.
According to Drik Panchang, the auspicious Raksha Bandhan shubh muhurat stretches for of 3 hours and 51 minutes, the thread ceremony is scheduled from 5:57 AM to 9:48 AM on August 28.
Quick answers to key questions
Raksha Bandhan is celebrated on 28 August 2026, which falls on a Friday.
Tying Rakhi on Raksha Bandhan symbolizes the bond of protection, love, and mutual respect between siblings, where sisters tie a sacred thread around their brothers' wrists and pray for their well-being.
The auspicious shubh muhurat for Raksha Bandhan in 2026 is from 5:57 AM to 9:48 AM, with the best time being during the Aparahna period if available.
Brothers give gifts to their sisters on Raksha Bandhan as a token of love and to pledge their protection and support through life's challenges.
Raksha Bandhan extends beyond biological siblings, as rakhis are also exchanged among cousins, friends, and neighbors, promoting harmony and mutual respect within the community.
“The best time to tie Rakhi on Raksha Bandhan is during Aparahna which is late afternoon according to Hindu division of the day. If Aparahna time is not available then Pradosh time is also suitable to perform rituals related to Raksha Bandhan. Raksha Bandhan rituals should not be done during Bhadra,” Drik Panchang states. As the Centre pushes to widen the role of AYUSH in India’s healthcare system — including through greater coverage, rural outreach and integration with mainstream health services — the country’s AYUSH medical education infrastructure has expanded rapidly.
But the expansion appears to have been driven largely by non-government institutions, according to government data.
India must use the AYUSH opportunity
The number of Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) colleges rose from 789 in 2021 to 971 in 2024, an increase of about 23%. Over the same period, total admission capacity grew from 63,477 to 79,593, or nearly 25%, while permitted seats grew from 50,711 to 72,490 — an increase of about 43%.
The 2021 figures cover Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Yoga and Naturopathy, Homoeopathy and Sowa-Rigpa. By April 2024, the Ministry registered 541 Ayurveda, 58 Unani, 17 Siddha, 71 Yoga and Naturopathy, 277 Homoeopathy and seven Sowa-Rigpa colleges.
Of the 541 Ayurveda colleges in April 2024, 467 were non-government — nearly 86% of the total. In Homoeopathy, 236 of 277 colleges, or about 85%, were non-government.
The pattern was similar in other systems. Of the 58 Unani colleges, only 16 were government-run; just three of 17 Siddha colleges and 15 of 71 Yoga and Naturopathy colleges were government institutions. Data clearly indicates that non-government institutions have become an important source of undergraduate medical education in AYUSH.
Additionally, the Ministry’s annual report for 2024-25 shows that 60,890 students were admitted against 63,073 permitted undergraduate seats in Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and Homoeopathy (ASU&H).
Ayurveda had almost full utilisation, with 39,952 of 40,136 permitted seats filled, Homoeopathy accounted for 1,887 vacancies — more than 86% of the total. The Ministry has also begun collecting admission data from State and Union Territory counselling authorities, improving the availability of national-level vacancy data.
Spending rises from a low base
Central spending under AYURGYAN, the Centre’s scheme supporting AYUSH education, capacity building, continuing medical education, research and innovation, has also increased.
The allocation rose from ₹8.42 crore in 2021-22 to ₹10.5 crore in 2022-23, ₹14.66 crore in 2023-24 and ₹48.5 crore in 2024-25, according to Ministry data placed before Parliament.
This, however, is not an education-only budget as AYURGYAN also supports capacity building and continuing medical education, research, and innovation; from 2023-24, it includes Ayurveda Biology Integrated Health Research.

Atletico Madrid hardened its stance over a possible sale of striker Julian Alvarez to Barcelona on Thursday, ruling out any negotiations with the Spanish champion.
The Atletico board “unanimously expressed their full support” for the club’s decision not to negotiate Alvarez’s transfer to Barcelona. However, the board indicated it is not closed off to other approaches, with Arsenal linked with the Argentina international in recent days.
“There has not been and there will not be any negotiation with them (Barcelona) regarding Alvarez’s transfer,” said Atletico in a statement.
The club said it was “open to negotiations inherent to the transfer market”, but only “in an ethical and professional manner and with respect between clubs”.
Atletico said Barcelona had not met those requirements, without providing further details. The Rojiblancos previously reported Barcelona to FIFA and the Spanish football federation for its pursuit of Alvarez.
Atletico said it is “convinced” Alvarez “will understand the decision, focusing on working in the best possible way to help the club achieve its objectives”.

The forward missed training for the second day running on Wednesday because of a reported illness, after being jeered by the club’s fans during Atletico’s 2-2 La Liga draw against Villarreal on Sunday.
Alvarez said in July during the World Cup that a transfer would be “best” for everyone.
“Julian is not doing well, because there are people that have been out to trick him, to confuse him,” Atletico CEO Miguel Angel Gil Marin told Movistar later Thursday.
“We are not going to negotiate with Barcelona under any circumstances,” he added.
Atletico’s club statement came a day after Barcelona president Joan Laporta said his club remained hopeful of signing 2022 World Cup winner Alvarez before the transfer window closes.
Laporta said Barca still had an offer, reported to be around 100 million euros ($116m), on the table for the 26-year-old.
Barcelona has made Alvarez its prime target as it seeks to strengthen its attack after the departures of Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres.
Alvarez joined Atletico from Manchester City in 2024 in a deal worth up to 95 million euros ($111m).
